Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the person will bear witness against himself as he reads his record, and Qatada adds that whoever could not read in this world will read that day. Al-Hasan considers that God has been just in making each person the reckoner of his own soul, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain 'hasib' as meaning one who reckons, or one who suffices as a witness. Readers differ on the vowels of 'yukhriju' and 'yalqahu', and Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi note that these variants do not change the core meaning. On the 'bird', Ibn 'Abbas takes it as what has been measured out for a person, Abu 'Ubayda as his share of fortune, and al-Hasan and Mujahid as the happiness or misery written for him. The following verses, in the commentators' reading, state that guidance benefits only the one who is guided, that straying harms only the one who strays, that no one bears another's burden, and that God does not punish a people until He has sent a messenger, which most take as punishment of annihilation in this world, while some extend it to the Hereafter.

This verse teaches that guidance and misguidance benefit or harm only the person who chooses them: whoever is guided gains for himself, whoever goes astray bears the consequence alone, and no one carries another's burden. It adds that God does not punish until He has sent a messenger to establish the proof. The commentators agree on this general meaning: each person is accountable for his own deeds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi stress that no one is punished for another's sin, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya also read it as a warning not to follow sin on the pretext that others committed it. On the phrase "We do not punish until We send a messenger," most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, take it to refer to worldly punishment, or punishment in general, once proof has been established. Al-Mawardi offers two readings, one based on revealed law and one based on reason. Al-Razi takes the verse to show that obligation rests on revelation, a view al-Zamakhshari disputes, holding that reason can establish the proof. On the fate of people living in periods without messengers and of children of unbelievers, opinions differ: some, such as al-Nawawi, hold that some of them are in Hell, others refrain from judging, and Ibn Kathir suggests they will be tested on the Day of Resurrection. Overall, the verse establishes God's justice, individual responsibility, and the necessity of a prior proof.

This verse explains that when God wills to destroy a town for its corruption, He commands its affluent and privileged people, the mutrafun, to obey through His messenger. They disobey and go out of obedience, so the sentence is fulfilled and the town is utterly destroyed. The commentators differ on the exact sense of the command. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Juzayy, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi take it to mean that God commanded them to obey and they disobeyed, and al-Shawkani also adopts this view. Al-Zamakhshari argues that the surface meaning is that they were commanded to commit debauchery, understood figuratively: abundant blessings led them to arrogance. Abu Hayyan, al-Razi and others reject this reading as unfitting for a passage meant to warn against misguidance. Ibn al-Qayyim treats the command as a cosmic decree rather than a religious law. Another reading takes the verb to mean multiplying: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and Abu Ubayda hold this view, citing the hadith about the fertile mare. Others understand it as empowering or appointing leaders, as reported from Mujahid, al-Rabi' and Abu al-Aliya. All agree that destruction means complete annihilation that leaves no trace. The verse also stresses that such punishment comes only after a messenger has been sent and proof given.

This verse tells us that Allah destroyed many generations after Noah, and it serves as a warning to the disbelievers of Quraysh: what befell those who denied their prophets could befall them too. It also affirms that Allah knows the sins of His servants perfectly and will hold them accountable. The commentators agree that the verse is a threat and that sins are the cause of destruction. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that Allah does not punish a people before sending them a messenger, a view Ibn 'Atiyya supports with reasoning and al-Razi finds consistent with the apparent sense. Scholars differ on the length of a qarn: Ibn Abi Awfa set it at a hundred and twenty years, others at a hundred, al-Kalbi at eighty and Ibn Sirin at forty. On the phrase « amarna mutrafiha », the majority take it as a command to obey that they disobeyed, al-Zamakhshari reads it figuratively as a command to sin, and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi takes it to mean multiplying their numbers, while some read it as making them rulers. Al-Farra' notes that the particle « bi » in « bi-rabbika » expresses praise. Al-Tabari adds that Allah does not strike a people with a punishment that does not fall on others, and that He judges each soul by its deeds.

This verse states that whoever desires only the hasty life of this world, and does not hope for the Hereafter, will be given in this world what God wills, and only to whom He wills, and then he will end up in Hell, burning there, blamed and cast away from mercy. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi agree that this worldly grant is restricted by God's will and choice, and that deprivation combined with punishment is the fate of one who prefers the present world. Al-Tabari and Qatada take "al-'ajila" to mean this life, while al-Fazari reads "whom We desire" as those whom God wills to destroy; al-Tabari adds that the verse targets the one who does not believe in the resurrection.

Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Shawkani note that the word "whoever desires" is general and includes disbelievers, sinners, hypocrites and those who show off, as well as the emigrant seeking worldly gain or the fighter seeking booty; Abu al-Su'ud follows this reading. Al-Qurtubi thinks the passage mainly concerns the hypocrites. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur stress that the desire for the Hereafter is not enough without striving and faith. Al-Razi lists three conditions for striving to be accepted: desiring the Hereafter, doing deeds that conform to the Law, and sincere faith.

Commentators also hold that the following verse, about God's provision to both groups, largely refers to worldly sustenance, according to Hasan al-Basri, Qatada and Ibn 'Atiyya, while Ibn 'Abbas understands it as obedient and disobedient deeds. The reading "yashā'" with ya, transmitted from Nafi', is noted, and the scholars differ on who the willing subject is.

This verse states that whoever desires the Hereafter, strives for it as it deserves, and is a believer, will have his striving accepted and rewarded by God. The commentators agree that faith is a necessary condition for an deed to be accepted. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi explain that God's thanks means accepting good deeds and overlooking bad ones, while al-Mawardi and al-Sam'ani understand it simply as the deed being accepted. Al-Razi lists three conditions: wanting the Hereafter, performing what is prescribed, and holding firm faith, quoting an early scholar who said that a deed lacking these three profits nothing. Al-Qurtubi notes that good deeds are accepted only from a believer and mentions a tradition about their multiplication. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud stress sincere intention and following the divine law rather than personal innovations. Several scholars, including Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Ashur, explain that the preceding verse concerns those who seek only the present life, and that God grants them a share of it according to His will. Ibn Kathir and al-Shinqiti conclude from this that an unbeliever's good works may be rewarded in this world alone. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya extend the idea to someone who seeks both the Hereafter and worldly goods. Ibn 'Ashur adds that wishing for the Hereafter's good without striving is not enough.

The commentators explain that God extends His bounty to both groups: those who desire the fleeting life of this world and those who desire the Hereafter. In this world He provides for the righteous and the wicked, the believer and the disbeliever alike, and their states diverge in the final outcome. Most agree that the 'bounty' here means worldly provision, and that the Hereafter belongs to the pious. Al-Tabari, with Ibn Zayd, al-Hasan and Qatada, holds that this provision covers all, and that 'not restricted' means not withheld; Qatada reads it as 'diminished', while Ibn 'Abbas takes it as 'prevented'. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that Ibn 'Abbas also understood the bounty as acts of obedience for those who seek the Hereafter and sins for those who seek this world, but he prefers the sense of livelihood. For the next verse, 'See how We have favoured some over others', most commentators point to differences in wealth, rank and health; al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir stress that the Hereafter holds far greater ranks and distinctions. Al-Razi sets out the conditions for the one who seeks the Hereafter: intending its reward through his deed, performing a lawful act, and being a believer, illustrating with the disbelievers whose practices are false. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Shawkani read the verse as a summary showing the breadth of God's mercy, even toward unbelievers in this life. All agree on the prohibition of associating partners with God that closes the passage, the phrase 'you will sit blamed and forsaken' being understood as remaining in blame and abandonment.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to reflect on how God has favoured some people over others in worldly provision and standing, and to understand that the distinction in the Hereafter is far greater. The commentators generally agree that the worldly distinction concerns wealth and circumstances, while the degrees and superiority in the next life depend on faith and deeds. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the people of Paradise differ in their ranks, the distance between two degrees being like that between heaven and earth, and that believers share the degrees according to their works. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the degrees of the Hereafter exceed anything that can be supposed, while he notes that some scholars took this distinction to apply only among believers. Al-Razi argues that the gap in the Hereafter relates to the worldly gap as the Hereafter relates to this world, and he also sees in the verse the superiority of believers in Paradise over unbelievers in the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi cite the episode in which Abu Sufyan and Suhayl ibn 'Amr complained about Bilal and Suhayb being admitted before them at the door of 'Umar, Suhayl replying that the distinction in the next life is far greater. Regarding the phrase 'Our gift', most commentators take it to mean worldly provision granted to both believers and disbelievers, whereas Ibn 'Abbas also understands it as including acts of obedience and disobedience. These differences leave the central meaning intact: conditions in this world are unequal, and the Hereafter offers a far greater elevation.

This verse forbids setting up another god alongside God. The commentators differ on who is addressed: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya take the address to be to the Prophet ﷺ, with the ruling meant for his community or for all those charged with the obligations of the faith, while al-Razi, al-Sam'ani and Abu al-Su'ud hold that it addresses the human being in general, al-Razi arguing that the following verses about parents cannot concern the Prophet, whose parents had died. The verb « taqʻuda » is read by al-Farra', al-Kisa'i and al-Zamakhshari as « become », so the sense is « you will become blamed and forsaken »; others, including Abu Hayyan, take it as « remain », or as incapacity, and al-Razi even allows a literal sitting in remorse. All agree that the blame comes from God, from the angels and from the believers, and that being forsaken means being left without help. Al-Tabari traces the blame to ingratitude for God's favours, and al-Razi traces the abandonment to relying on a non-existent partner. Ibn al-Qayyim states that whoever attaches himself to other than God is the most forsaken of people, while Ibn Sa'di adds that the one who professes the oneness of God is praised and helped in every situation. The commentators agree that the verse establishes the basic prohibition of polytheism.

The commentators explain that the verse states God's decree and command that people worship Him alone and show kindness to their parents, a kindness that becomes especially binding when they reach old age and need care. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Kathir understand the verb qadā as meaning command or enjoin; Mujahid, al-Dahhak and others report the reading wa-wassā (he enjoined), which al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi consider contrary to consensus. Nearly all agree that forbidding the word uff covers every form of harm. On the meaning of uff, Mujahid and 'Ata' take it as expressing disgust at filth, as the parents once cleaned the child, al-Asma'i connects it with ear wax, al-Khalil with fingernail dirt, and Muqatil with coarse speech. Ibn al-Musayyab defines the gracious word as that of a guilty slave to a harsh master. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi link filial duty to gratitude toward God, the ultimate source of existence. As for praying for the parents, Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas hold it abrogated by the verse forbidding prayers for forgiveness for polytheists, while others limit it to believing parents or see no abrogation. On the question of jihad, al-Thawri requires the parents' permission, whereas al-Shafi'i permits it without it.

This verse tells the son to lower to his parents the wing of humility out of mercy, that is, to be gentle and submissive towards them, and to pray: "My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small." The commentators link it to the command to worship God alone and to be good to one's parents. They largely agree that it means obeying them in what is not sinful, speaking and acting with courtesy, praying for them, and showing them particular gentleness in old age. Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain "the wing of humility" as an image taken from a bird lowering its wing over its young, and treat the phrase as a figure of speech for humility, while others understand it simply as humility. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Asim read "al-dhill" with a kasra, which al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi relate to the meaning of docility. On praying for the parents, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid consider the verse abrogated by the prohibition of asking forgiveness for polytheists, whereas al-Razi and al-Baydawi hold that it applies to believing parents or may include asking God to guide non-believing parents. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir cite many hadiths on the merit of filial piety and the gravity of disobedience, including the saying that God's pleasure lies in the pleasure of the parents.

This verse states that God knows best what lies in people's hearts, whether it is goodness toward parents or disobedience toward them. If one's intention is sound and a lapse occurs, God forgives the one who returns to Him in repentance. The commentators agree in warning against harboring ill will toward parents and in promising forgiveness to those whose intentions are upright. The meaning of 'awwabin' (those who turn back) is explained in several ways. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada understand them as those who glorify God, who obey Him, or who pray; Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab describes someone who sins, repents, sins again and repents again; Mujahid and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr take it to mean one who recalls his sins in private and asks forgiveness; 'Awn al-'Uqayli and Ibn al-Munkadir see them as those who pray the forenoon prayer or the prayer between sunset and nightfall. Al-Tabari prefers the view that the awwab is the one who returns from disobedience to obedience, a meaning drawn from the root meaning 'to return'. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya add that the verse may apply to anyone who has erred and repented, including a child who has wronged his parents. According to Sa'id ibn Jubayr, the verse concerns a sudden outburst toward a parent without any intention of harm. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi specify that the lapse may occur in a moment of anger or distress.

This verse commands giving the near relative his due, along with the needy and the traveller, and forbids squandering wealth. The majority of commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya, understand the near relative as a person's own kin on the father's and mother's side, and the due as maintaining family ties, giving financial help when needed and offering every kind of support. Ali ibn al-Husayn and al-Sudi report that it refers to the relatives of the Prophet ﷺ, whose share should come from the public treasury or the khums; al-Zamakhshari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi mention this view without deciding between the two. Al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya prefer the first reading, since the verse links this due to the needy and the traveller and God restricts no right in particular.

The needy (miskin) is the destitute person humbled by poverty, and the traveller (ibn al-sabil) is one cut off from his wealth. Some say his due is hospitality for three days, a mount, or help to continue his journey. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy report that Abu Hanifa requires supporting poor, unable-to-work relatives within the prohibited degrees, while al-Shafi'i limits the obligation of maintenance to parents and children.

On squandering, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas, followed by Qatada, define it as spending wealth wrongly or in disobedience. Mujahid holds that giving all one's wealth to a right cause is not squandering, while giving a single mudd for a wrong purpose is. Al-Mawardi distinguishes extravagance (israf), which exceeds the amount, from squandering (tabdhir), which misplaces the spending; al-Zamakhshari considers the latter to include the former. The verse says squanderers are brothers of the devils, meaning their likes, companions or allies, or their fellows in the Fire, according to the interpretations transmitted.

This part of the verse states that those who squander, meaning those who spend their wealth wrongly and in disobedience or extravagance, are brothers of the devils, meaning their likes, companions or followers, and that the devil was ungrateful to his Lord. The commentators agree that squandering means spending money in a wrong place, as reported from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi explain that 'brothers' may mean a resemblance in evil, companionship and following, or fellow inmates of the Fire as a warning. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Shawkani stress the severity of this resemblance, since there is no evil worse than the devil's. Abu al-Su'ud notes that singling out ingratitude shows that squandering means diverting God's blessings from their purpose, which is a form of ingratitude opposed to thankfulness. Ibn 'Ashur sees a warning that habit can gradually lead to disbelief. Al-Qurtubi reports that the Malikis allow restraining a spendthrift when his wealth is at risk of running out, while Abu Hanifa does not accept restraint for squandering. Al-Tabari extends the point to anyone who spends his wealth in disobedience to God.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ that when he must turn away from relatives, the needy, or the traveller because he has nothing to give, and hopes for mercy from his Lord, he should answer them with gentle and kind words. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, along with most early commentators, explain that waiting means awaiting provision, and that the mercy is the sustenance hoped for, while the easy word is a good promise such as: God will provide, and I will give you. Al-Hasan and Qatada understand it as soft and gentle speech. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud note that turning away may mean being unable to help, and that the phrase may invoke God's blessing. Ibn Zayd holds that the refusal came from fear that the recipient would spend the gift in disobedience, so the mercy means repentance; al-Tabari finds this reading far from the apparent meaning. Reports of the occasion of revelation mention poor companions who asked the Prophet, or men of Muzayna who asked for a mount. Several commentators, including al-Qurtubi, present the verse within the teaching of moderation between miserliness and extravagance. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas define extravagance as spending outside what is right, while Mujahid holds that giving all one's wealth in what is right is not extravagance.

This verse warns against both extremes of stinginess and extravagance. A person should not keep the hand so tight that it seems chained to the neck, nor open it so wide that nothing remains, leaving him blamed and empty-handed. Most commentators understand the verse this way. Al-Tabari, citing al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, reads it as a warning against both miserliness and squandering, and Ibn Kathir follows the same reading, attributed to Ibn Abbas. Al-Tabari explains that the word for "stripped bare" comes from the image of an exhausted camel that can no longer walk, while Qatada takes it to mean full of regret. Ibn al-Jawzi quotes Ibn Qutayba, who compares a person who gives away everything to a traveller whose mount has collapsed and is left stranded. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi present the verse as a pair of images, one for the miser and one for the spendthrift, urging the moderate path between them. Al-Razi frames it through the ethical principle that virtue lies in the mean between two vices. Al-Qurtubi notes that Mujahid considered giving all of one's wealth for a good cause not to be wasteful, while Ibn Atiyya follows Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud in defining waste as spending on what is not right. The story of the boy who asks the Prophet for his shirt, reported by al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi, is mentioned by several commentators, although Ibn Hajar and others question its authenticity. The commentators agree that God alone extends or restricts provision as He knows best for each of His servants.

In this verse God tells His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that his Lord extends provision to whom He wills among His servants and restricts it for whom He wills, and that He is aware of His servants' inner states and sees their outward conditions, knowing what suits each of them. The commentators read the verse in the context of the preceding verses, which forbid both stinginess and extravagance. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand that expansion and restriction belong to God alone, so the Prophet, like anyone else, is not required to give without limit, since the distribution of wealth depends on His will. They agree that the verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ for the insistence of those who asked of him and the scarcity of what he had, and that God did not withhold provision from him out of contempt or miserliness. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain that the differences in income follow wisdom and benefit, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that turning away from a petitioner was due to being unable to give, not to rejection. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also report that God knows whom abundance would benefit and whom it would harm, since some are corrupted by ease while others are improved by it. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi add that wealth may be a test for some and poverty a punishment for others, a point the remaining commentators do not take up. In short, the commentators agree that the distribution of provision rests on divine wisdom and that the believer should seek moderation, neither wasteful nor miserly.

This verse forbids killing children out of fear of poverty, and states that God provides for the children as well as for their parents, and that killing them is a great sin. Most commentators explain that the word imlaq means poverty and destitution, and they report that the pre-Islamic Arabs buried their daughters alive for fear of want, with al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya citing Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas on this practice. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the prohibition covers both sons and daughters, while Ibn 'Ashur explains that the verse mainly addresses the killing of daughters. There is general agreement that the word khit'an means a grave sin, though scholars differ on its nuances. Al-Tabari, al-Farra and Abu 'Ubayda treat the forms khit' and khata' as near-synonyms, whereas al-Raghib, al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Mawardi distinguish khit', a deliberate fault, from khata', an unintentional error. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi simply render the word as a great sin. Several readings are recorded, such as khata', khita' and khita, but most commentators regard them as variants of closely related meaning. Al-Razi links the verse to the preceding one about provision, and Ibn 'Ashur observes that the phrase 'We provide for them and for you' stresses divine providence. Modern commentators such as Sayyid Qutb and al-Sha'rawi stress that belief in God as sole provider put an end to this practice.

This verse forbids fornication and tells believers to keep away from anything that leads to it. The commentators stress that the phrase "do not draw near" is stronger than "do not commit", because it covers preliminaries and everything that leads to the act. They describe fornication as an act of extreme ugliness that goes beyond what is acceptable, and its path as an evil path that leads to the Fire. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Sam'ani consider the meaning plain: it is a great sin and a bad way. Al-Razi lists several reasons for its gravity, among them the confusion of lineages, the neglect of children and the quarrels it sparks, while Ibn al-Qayyim holds that it gathers every kind of evil and cites many hadiths on its consequences, such as the loss of the face's radiance and a shortened life.

The commentators agree that fornication is one of the major sins and that its ugliness is beyond dispute. The readers differed over the pronunciation of the word "zina", some reading the short form and others the long form, which lexicographers say is attested among some Arabs. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi note that the prohibition covers preliminaries such as touching and kissing. Ibn 'Ashur links the verse to the prohibition of infanticide, since fornication can destroy lineage and leave children without a clear parent, much as burying daughters does.

Al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di stress that the prohibition protects families and society. Sayyid Qutb and al-Sha'rawi develop the same point, emphasising the role of lineage and marriage in social stability. Some scholars differed on whether the verse is Meccan or Medinan, al-Dahhak holding that the passage on killing is Meccan, while Ibn 'Ashur rejected the claim that this verse is Medinan.

This verse of Surat al-Isra' forbids taking a life that God has made sacred, except by right. The commentators, following Ibn 'Abbas, explain that the right to kill is limited to three cases: apostasy after faith, adultery by one who is married, and deliberate unjust killing. When a person is killed unjustly, God gives the victim's heir, the wali, an authority (sultan) to claim justice. The commentators differ on what this authority means. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak take it as a choice between retaliation, accepting blood money, and pardon, while Qatada takes it as retaliation alone. Al-Tabari adopts Ibn 'Abbas's view, supported by a hadith from the conquest of Mecca.

The exegetes agree that excess in retaliation is forbidden. Most describe it as killing someone other than the murderer, a custom of the pre-Islamic Arabs who would kill a noble member of the killer's tribe for a single slain man. Mujahid, Qatada and Talq ibn Habib add mutilating the killer, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr adds killing several people for one. Al-Tabari holds that the two readings, with the second and third person, are both valid.

The pronoun at the end, "he was helped", is read in different ways. Qatada and most others refer it to the wali, whom God supports by granting him retaliation. Mujahid refers it to the victim, whom God helps in this world through retaliation and in the next through reward. Al-Tabari prefers the wali, while Ibn 'Atiyya finds the victim more likely, since the word "help" naturally contrasts with injustice.

This verse tells believers not to touch an orphan's property except in the best way, which the commentators explain as guarding it and making it grow, until the orphan reaches his maturity. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the best way as guarding and investing the wealth in the orphan's interest. Ibn 'Atiyya adds that the guardian may take a modest, reasonable share for his effort, and that this is a matter of lawful wage. Mujahid allows a guardian who is poor to borrow from the property and repay it, while Ibn 'Abbas and Zayd ibn Aslam allow eating with propriety, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab forbids it altogether. Several report that when the verse was revealed the Companions became reluctant to mix their food with orphans, until the verse of al-Baqara relieved them. On maturity (ashudd), the commentators differ: most say puberty or eighteen years, others mention thirty-three, and al-Razi defines it as the completion of reason and strength. On the covenant, all agree that it is binding, whether between a person and God or between people, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that the wording may be a rhetorical personification, rebuking the one who breaks it. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi relate the duty to fulfil measure and weight, which some read as the balance or justice. The passage closes with the prohibition on speaking without knowledge, since hearing, sight and heart will be questioned about it.

This verse commands giving full measure when measuring for others and weighing with a true, straight balance, and it declares this better and finer in outcome. The commentators agree on the core point: the buyer's right must be met completely, without cheating or shortfall, and justice in exchange is the heart of the matter. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the phrase "better in outcome" means better in return, reward and final end, both in this life and in the next. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi note that the duty to measure falls on the seller, since the command to give full measure is addressed to the one who measures out the goods.

Scholars differ on the meaning of the word "qistas". Al-Hasan takes it to be the steelyard (al-qabban), al-Zajjaj to be any scale, small or large, and Mujahid to be justice in the Roman tongue, while others such as al-Razi regard it as an Arabic word derived from the root for justice, qist. The readers vary in the first vowel: Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read it with a kasra, and the rest with a damma, both accepted as valid forms. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the verse speaks of a straight balance because an accurate scale almost always prevents injustice, whereas measuring by volume is more easily exposed to cheating.

This verse tells people not to follow what they have no knowledge of, whether in speech or action, and to verify before speaking or acting. The commentators explain that a person will be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about how he used his hearing, sight and heart, and that these faculties will bear witness against him. Qatada and, in one report, Ibn Abbas, together with Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, understood it as a prohibition on saying 'I saw' when one has not seen, 'I heard' when one has not heard, or 'I know' when one does not know, and on giving false testimony. Mujahid and, in another report, Ibn Abbas read it as a prohibition on accusing people without basis, noting that the root qafw means slander. Al-Qutaybi took it to mean not following guesses and conjecture. Several scholars, including al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, favoured a general sense covering all these meanings. Al-Zamakhshari held that the verse also reaches imitation without knowledge, while others argued that a strong probable judgment may stand in place of knowledge and that the text does not exclude this. On grammar, some say the pronoun in 'about it' refers to each faculty, others to its owner, and the use of 'those' for inanimate things is supported by a line of Jarir. The following verses forbid arrogance and associating partners with God, which the commentators treat as principles of the wisdom revealed to the Prophet.

This verse forbids walking on the earth with arrogance and swagger. The commentators explain that maraḥ means excessive joy in vain things, or boastfulness and conceit in one's gait. The verse reminds the human being that he can neither split the earth beneath his feet nor reach the height of the mountains, so his pride brings him nothing. Al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Kathir read it as a prohibition of vanity and pride, while al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Baydawi see in it a mocking rebuke of the one who struts. Al-Razi notes that man is weak, surrounded by earth below and mountains above, so pride does not suit him. The scholars agree that the exhortation is general, although it is addressed to the Prophet.

The passage then summarises the earlier commands and prohibitions. The readings differ: Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read sayyi'atan with tanwin, making all the prohibited acts a single evil hateful to God, while Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read sayyi'uhu, meaning that the evil part of these acts is what is hateful. Al-Tabari and al-Razi prefer the second reading, since the passage mixes commands and prohibitions. Al-Qurtubi notes that Ubayy's reading supports it. The verse closes with a warning against associating other gods with God, which leads to Hell, blamed and cast away.

The commentators explain that this verse closes a long series of commands and prohibitions that began with 'Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him'. Its plain meaning is that every one of these matters, in its blameworthy aspect, namely what is forbidden, is detested in the sight of God, who does not approve of it or command it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that the reading 'sayyi'uhu', in the construct form, means that the commands contain both good and bad, so only their bad part is hated, while the reading 'sayyi'atan', with tanwin, refers only to the prohibitions. Al-Tabari prefers the first reading, and Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zajjaj also consider it the better reading. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain that God's hatred does not mean that He does not will these acts, since everything happens by His will, whereas al-Qadi takes the hatred to mean prohibition. Al-Zamakhshari explains the feminine form by the fact that 'sayyi'a' functions like the noun 'sin', so its gender is disregarded. Commentators connect the passage to the rejection of polytheism, disobedience to parents, killing, extravagance and arrogance, all presented as wisdom revealed to the Prophet.

This verse states that the commands and prohibitions set out earlier in the sura are part of the wisdom that God revealed to His Prophet, and that the root of all this wisdom is not to set up any other god beside God. Whoever does so will be cast into Hell, blamed and driven away. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the one blamed is someone whom his own soul and people will reproach, and that the one driven away is the rejected and banished, an explanation also given by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada. Al-Samani and al-Baghawi hold that the address is to the Prophet while the intended audience is the community, a view Ibn Kathir repeats while noting that the Prophet is protected from sin. Al-Mawardi links the repetition of admonitions to their variety, so that people may take heed. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that wisdom refers to firm rulings that are never abrogated, and they report from Ibn 'Abbas that these verses were on the tablets of Moses, with monotheism as the foundation of all wisdom. Al-Razi distinguishes between the blamed and the despised, and between the forsaken and the repelled, placing blame and rejection in the Hereafter. Al-Qurtubi clarifies that casting means throwing something down from a height and implies humiliation.

This verse rebukes those who claimed that the angels are God's daughters. God asks them, in a tone of reproach, whether your Lord chose sons for you while taking daughters from the angels for Himself. They attribute to God what they dislike for themselves and reserve for Him the lesser share. The commentators agree that the address is to the Arab polytheists, that the interrogative particle expresses denial and rebuke, and that the verb asfa means to single out or to prefer. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that the Arabs sometimes buried their daughters and regarded female births with disdain, which makes their position inconsistent. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi argue that this contradicts wisdom and even human custom, since masters do not give their servants the best and keep the worst for themselves. Al-Razi adds that ascribing offspring to God implies composition and division, which conflicts with His eternity and necessary existence. Al-Qurtubi reports an opinion that the verse addresses the Jews, but most scholars take it to address the polytheists of Mecca. All agree that the phrase qawlan 'aziman describes a statement monstrous in its impiety and gravity. Ibn 'Ashur links the passage to the prohibition of association that precedes it, since worship of the angels was among the practices of some Arabs.

This verse says that God explained in the Quran, through proofs, lessons, parables, and admonitions, and repeated its themes in varied forms, so that the idolaters might remember, understand their error, and turn away from their ignorance. The commentators agree, however, that this clarity only increased their aversion to the truth. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that “nufur” means fleeing from the truth and keeping away from it, and Ibn 'Atiyya compares it to the bolting of a startled animal. The common reading “sarrafna” with doubled letter signifies multiplication, while al-Hasan reads it without doubling. Al-Mawardi, al-Sam'ani and al-Razi offer two meanings: repeating the admonitions, or varying their forms and kinds. Al-Qurtubi also reports that it may refer to the Quran being sent down gradually. On “li-yadhdhakkaru”, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read “yadhkurū”, while Abu 'Ubayd prefers the doubled form, meaning to reflect and take heed. The verse is followed by an argument on monotheism: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi explain that if there were other gods alongside God they would seek a path to Him in nearness, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari also mention the interpretation of rival kings contending for power.

God tells His Prophet to say to the polytheists that sound reasoning refutes the claim of many gods: if there were other deities with Him, as they claim, those deities would seek a way to the Lord of the Throne, that is, to God, who holds sovereignty and lordship. The commentators differ on what this seeking means. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, and Qatada understand it as seeking nearness to God and a place in His favour, since such deities would be subordinate to Him and in need of Him, so worshipping them instead of Him makes no sense. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu 'Ali al-Farisi, al-Naqqash, and Abu Mansur take it to mean struggling against Him to overthrow His rule, as kings contend with one another. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, and Abu al-Su'ud regard this second reading as the more apparent one, and it links the verse to the argument from mutual rivalry stated elsewhere in the Qur'an. The verse ends by declaring God exalted far above what they say. The commentators agree that the heavens, the earth, and all within them glorify Him. They differ on how literal this is: some take it as the real praise of every thing, others as the evidence that creatures give of their Creator, and others restrict it to rational beings, to living things, or to growing plants. All agree that God is Forbearing and Forgiving, who delays punishment and pardons whoever repents.

This verse declares God far exalted above what the polytheists attribute to Him, namely partners and daughters. The commentators explain that it is a glorification and an exaltation of God beyond such claims, for none of what they ascribe to Him belongs to His attributes or befits Him. The following verse, closely linked to it, says that the seven heavens, the earth and whatever is in them glorify God, including angels, humans and jinn. Al-Tabari transmits from Qatada, Ikrima and al-Hasan that every living thing glorifies God, that a tree does so while a pillar does not, and that food was heard glorifying God while being eaten. Ibn Kathir holds, on the best-known view, that the glorification is general, covering animals, plants and inanimate things, and he cites reports of food and pebbles glorifying God. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi, by contrast, take the glorification of inanimate things as an indication through their state, a sign of the Creator, and they note that the verse says people do not understand this glorification. Al-Qurtubi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Jaza'iri lean toward reading the verse as addressing human understanding rather than the speech of objects. Ibn Hazm, cited by al-Qasimi, argues that the word is shared between two meanings, one proper to humans and another proper to things. Ibn 'Ashur reads the exaltation as a real declaration of God's transcendence rather than a mere claim. All agree on God's purity from any partner or child; they differ on the real nature of the glorification of beings without reason.

God is exalted above what the polytheists attribute to Him, and the seven heavens, the earth, and all who dwell in them, whether angels, humans or jinn, glorify Him; there is nothing that does not praise Him, yet people do not grasp their glorification. The commentators agree on the general sense: this glorification proclaims the greatness of the Creator and His exaltation above defects and partners, and it testifies to His oneness through creation.

They differ on its nature. Al-Tabari keeps the broad meaning of 'thing' and reports, with other early transmitters, that this glorification belongs to everything that has life; Qatada, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak restrict it to living beings, animals and plants. Ikrima says a tree glorifies God while a pillar does not, and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i includes food and the creak of a door among the things that glorify Him. Al-Mawardi lists three views: only living beings, everything that exists, or glorification as the trace of the work's marvel that moves the beholder to praise God.

Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur take this glorification figuratively, as the language of state: every creature demonstrates by its contingency the existence of a necessary, wise Creator, and the phrase 'you do not understand' then addresses the polytheists who failed to reflect. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Tha'alibi and Abu al-Su'ud prefer a literal glorification, supported by reports of food and pebbles glorifying God. Al-Razi finds the literal reading difficult, since it implies speech from inanimate things, and he keeps the first interpretation.

The closing phrase, 'He is Forbearing and Forgiving', is read by most as meaning that God does not hasten punishment against disobedient people and pardons those who repent.

This verse says that when the Prophet ﷺ recites the Qur'an to the disbelievers who deny the Hereafter, God places between him and them a veil that keeps their hearts from understanding and benefiting from it, as a punishment for their disbelief. The commentators differ on what this veil is. Qatada, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir, with al-Zajjaj, understand it as the coverings over the hearts, an inner barrier that prevents understanding; al-Tabari also takes this to be the clearer meaning in the context. Others, such as al-Kalbi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi, report that the veil was a physical screen that hid the Prophet from the enemies' sight, drawing on the account of Abu Lahab's wife; al-Qurtubi regards this as the more apparent meaning. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi link the veil to the seal placed upon the hearts. As for the word masturan, it may mean 'that which covers', as al-Akhfash, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi hold, or 'hidden from sight', or 'itself veiled'; al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi set out these variants. Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Ashur stress that the turning away comes from the unbelievers' own refusal to listen. Several accounts of the occasion of revelation, linked to the sura of Al-Masad, are widely cited, though their weight in interpreting the verse is debated among the exegetes.

This verse says that God placed coverings over the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter, so they cannot grasp the Qur'an, and deafness in their ears, so they cannot hear it in a way that benefits them, and that when the Prophet recites the Qur'an, God places a veil between him and them. Most commentators read this as an image of their misguidance and their inability to benefit from the Qur'an, a punishment for their disbelief and refusal. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy take the phrase 'lest they understand it' to mean 'out of aversion'. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari take the veil to be the coverings over the hearts, and al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir favour the view that it is hidden from sight, whereas al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj read 'concealed' as 'concealing'. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that it may also be a protection against harm at night or a concealment from sight. As for 'when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an', most take it to mean the declaration 'there is no god but God' or the affirmation of divine oneness, which makes the polytheists flee because it rejects their idols. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-Jawza' say the ones who turn away are the devils, while al-Tabari holds that they are the polytheists. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi report several occasions of revelation, some involving Abu Lahab and his wife, others the gatherings where the Quraysh listened to the Qur'an.

This verse states that God knows best what the polytheists seek when they listen to the Prophet ﷺ reciting: they listen to mock and reject, not to be guided, and God knows their secret whispering, when the wrongdoers say to one another that they follow only a man who has been bewitched. The commentators agree on the general sense but differ on the word "masḥūr". Al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj, Ibn Qutayba and al-Baghawi take it to mean a man deceived, or whose mind has been clouded by magic, an interpretation already attributed to Mujahid. Abu 'Ubayda understood it as a man who has a "sihr", that is a lung, and so is a human who eats and drinks like them, citing verses of al-Imru' al-Qays and Labid. Ibn Qutayba judged this reading strained and preferred the first. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi keep the sense of a man struck by sorcery, and Ibn 'Atiyya regards it as the most likely reading. On the particle "bihi", some take it as causal, others as superfluous, and others as describing a circumstance meaning mocking. The exegetes report that these secret talks included insults against the Prophet: sorcerer, soothsayer, poet or madman. Ibn Kathir narrates that Abu Sufyan, al-Akhnas and Abu Jahl secretly listened by night. Several commentators link this passage to the preceding verses, which describe the veil placed over the hearts of those who turn away.

God tells His Prophet to look with insight at the contradictory descriptions the disbelievers gave him: they likened him to a poet, a sorcerer, a soothsayer and a madman, and in going astray through these claims they found no way out of their confusion. The commentators explain that the "way" here means the path of guidance, and some add that they could not escape their own contradictions. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the verse was revealed about al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and his companions, and that the "similitudes" are these labels hurled at the Prophet. On the word "mashur", opinions differ: Ibn Qutayba, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to mean deceived, Abu 'Ubayda takes it to mean a man who has a windpipe, that is, one who eats and drinks like them, while Ibn al-Qayyim holds that it means one whose mind has been disturbed, and he rejects the reading of the windpipe. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir relate that the polytheists made these remarks in their private conversations while listening to the Qur'an. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi describe this error as that of a person lost in the desert who does not know which road to take. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the plural "similitudes" fits because their astonishment concerns all their remarks. The commentators do not settle between these views and present them to the reader.

This verse reports the denial of resurrection by the Meccan unbelievers: how could we be raised once we have become bones and dust? The commentators agree that the question is one of astonishment and rejection, judging a new creation after annihilation to be implausible. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy explain that 'rufat' means dust, powder or fragments, citing Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. On the phrase 'be stones or iron', al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as a challenge showing they could not escape God even if they were the hardest substances, while Ibn Juzayy and al-Alusi see an imagined supposition, and al-Razi holds that life can return even to what is furthest from it. On 'a creation greater in your breasts', most exegetes, including Ibn Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir, identify it as death; others, including Mujahid in one report, name the heavens, the earth and the mountains, and al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi present these views without deciding. Ibn 'Atiyya considers the referral to their innate nature more sound, a view al-Tabari also prefers. All agree on the answer to 'who will bring us back?': the one who created them the first time is able to do so. Their question 'when?' is mockery, and the reply is that it is near, on a day when they will answer by praising God and think they had stayed only a little while.

God instructs His Prophet to answer those who deny the resurrection and find it hard to believe that they will be re-created after becoming bones and dust. He tells them: be stones or iron, or a creation even greater in your minds for accepting life. Many commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, read this as a challenge meant to show their helplessness: even if you were the furthest thing from life, God would still be able to bring you back, since nothing limits Him. Al-Tabari stresses that the sense is: if you are astonished that God creates you from bones and flesh, then become stones yourselves if you can, while Ibn Kathir and others explain that He will make you die and then raise you. As for the creation that is greater in your breasts, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Dahhak and most exegetes say it is death, since nothing is greater in the human soul. Mujahid says it means the heavens, the earth and the mountains, and Qatada means anything great in their eyes, with al-Tabari preferring the general sense. God then tells the Prophet to answer those who ask who will restore them: the One who created them the first time. They shake their heads mockingly and ask when this will happen; the answer is that it is near, since God's 'perhaps' is a certainty. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada explain the shaking of heads as mockery. Scholars differ on 'the day He calls you': some take it as the final blast, others as an address to believers. Most take 'praising Him' to mean responding by His command or with knowledge and obedience, and the sense of having stayed only a little refers either to the time between the two blasts, to life in this world, or to the feeling on the Day of Resurrection.

The commentators explain that this verse answers those who denied resurrection and found it hard to believe that a person could live again after becoming bones and dust. God tells His Prophet to say: be stones or iron, or some creation even greater in your hearts, and God can still bring you back to life. The commentators differ on what this great creation is. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada and al-Dahhak take it to be death, meaning that even if you were death itself, God would give you life. Mujahid says it refers to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, and al-Kalbi says it is the resurrection itself. Qatada takes it to mean anything that impresses the human mind. Al-Tabari concludes that the verse includes whatever is great in the hearts of the children of Adam, since it specifies nothing.

All agree on the reply: the One who created you the first time can recreate you, since whoever can originate can also restore. Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi read the words "be" as a challenge rather than a command, and al-Razi presents the argument that God is never overcome by matter. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that bones are the framework of a living body, so their return to life is no marvel. The verb "yunghidun", to shake the head, is understood as a gesture of mockery or denial.

Finally, "perhaps it is near" is understood by al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Nasafi and al-Razi as a certainty coming from God, meaning the Hour is close. Al-Razi adds that nearness is relative, since what remains of the world's duration is less than what has passed.

This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when God calls people out of their graves and they respond obediently, praising Him, while believing they had stayed only a short time, overwhelmed by what they see. The commentators differ on the sense of "bihamdihi". Ibn Abbas, Ibn Juraij, al-Kalbi and al-Zajjaj take it as "by His command", Qatada as "through knowledge and obedience of Him", and Sa'id ibn Jubayr reports that they rise saying "Glory be to You and praise be to You". Al-Tabari reads it as "and praise belongs to God", while al-Zamakhshari sees a hyperbole about their submission to being raised. On the verb "you think", al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as conjecture, whereas Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan allow that it may mean certainty. As for "only a little", opinions vary: the interval between the two blasts of the trumpet, forty years according to al-Kalbi and al-Razi, during which punishment is lifted from the disbelievers; the life of this world according to al-Hasan and Qatada; or the period in the grave according to Muqatil. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take the verse to address disbelievers, while al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy leave open that it may address believers.

God instructs His Prophet to tell the believing servants to speak to one another in the best and gentlest manner, because Satan stirs up discord and enmity among them, and he has been man's open enemy since the story of Adam. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the command as avoiding harshness in speech, al-Hasan al-Basri adding that one may say to an unbeliever «May God guide you» or «May God have mercy on you». Ibn 'Atiyya takes it as a general instruction to believers among themselves. The commentators differ on who is addressed: most, including al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, hold that believers are speaking to polytheists, while al-Tabari and others take it as addressing believers to one another. Al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi offer several readings of the best word: affirming what the Prophet brought, enjoining good and forbidding evil, returning good for insult, or the declaration that there is no god but God, which Ibn Sirin reports. Several accounts link the revelation to the insults suffered by Muslims, or to an incident involving 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. Some hold the verse abrogated by the verse of the sword, while Ibn Kathir rejects any abrogation. The passage adds that the Prophet is not a guardian charged with compelling people to believe.

This verse tells us that the Lord knows people best. If He wills, He will show them mercy by guiding them to faith and repentance, and if He wills, He will punish them by leaving them to die in disbelief. The Prophet was not sent as a guardian who forces people to believe, but as one who delivers the message. Most commentators agree that the verse addresses the Quraysh who denied resurrection. According to Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, mercy means being guided to faith, and punishment means dying in polytheism. Others, such as al-Kalbi and Ibn al-Jawzi, hold that the address is to the believers: mercy would then mean their deliverance from the Meccan unbelievers, and punishment their subjugation by them. Al-Mawardi gives three possible meanings, including guidance versus misguidance, deliverance from enemies versus their domination, and repentance versus persistence in sin, the last one reported from al-Hasan. As for the word wakil, al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi understand it as one who compels or as a guarantor, and al-Mawardi and al-Sam'ani cite a line of poetry to support the meaning of guarantor. Several scholars, including al-Nahhas and al-Baghawi, consider the verse abrogated by the verse of fighting, while others regard it as still valid. Al-Razi and al-Biqa'i connect the passage to what precedes it: arguments should be presented without insult, since abuse stirs up strife. Most commentators interpret the phrase the best word as courteous speech, such as saying may God guide you or may God have mercy on you. Accounts of the occasion of revelation differ, from an insult directed at Umar ibn al-Khattab to the Muslims' complaints about the persecution they suffered from the polytheists, and the commentators do not settle the question.

This verse states that your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and on earth, that He preferred some prophets over others, and that He gave David the Psalms (al-Zabur). The commentators explain that this preference rests on gifts specific to each prophet, such as the intimate friendship granted to Abraham, the direct speech with Moses, the raising of the dead through Jesus, or the kingship of Solomon, and not on wealth or the number of followers. Al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Juzayy read it as a reply to the Meccans who found it hard to accept that an orphan of Abu Talib could be a prophet, since God alone knows who is fit for the mission. Qatada describes the Zabur as a collection of supplications, praise and glorification, with no lawful or unlawful rulings, no obligations and no penalties. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi hold that mentioning David points to the superiority of the Prophet ﷺ, because the Zabur foretells that the righteous servants will inherit the earth, which they link to his community. Ibn Kathir distinguishes a preference grounded in divine knowledge from one driven by whim or partisanship, citing the hadith forbidding preference among prophets out of vanity. He holds that messengers are above other prophets, that the steadfast messengers are the most excellent, with Muhammad ﷺ first, then Abraham and Moses according to the best-known view. Al-Razi observes that naming David shows the preference concerns knowledge and religion rather than kingship, and that the Zabur answered Jews who claimed no book would follow the Torah. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the verse dismisses the polytheists' doubts about the Prophet's mission, since preference among prophets is a established divine practice.

This verse tells the Prophet to say to the idolaters: call upon those you claim to be gods besides Him, for they cannot remove the harm that afflicts you, nor transfer it to anyone else. The commentators agree that the verse answers those who worshipped beings other than God in the belief that these would bring them closer to Him. They differ, however, on who these beings were. Ibn Mas'ud, reported by al-Tabari, says they were groups of jinn who embraced Islam while their worshippers remained unbelievers. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others name Jesus, his mother, 'Uzayr and the angels, some adding the sun, the moon and the stars; al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd name the angels. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir find Ibn Mas'ud's view the strongest, since the verse speaks of an event in the Prophet's time, which cannot apply to Jesus or 'Uzayr, while al-Tabari also accepts the angels. Al-Razi stresses the helplessness of these beings and argues that only one who can remove harm deserves worship. The next verse, according to the majority reading, states that these same beings seek nearness to their Lord, hope for His mercy and fear His punishment, which shows they cannot be divine. Commentators understand the wasila as nearness gained through obedience, and the fear of God's punishment as something everyone should guard against.

This verse explains that those whom the polytheists called upon besides God, whether angels, the Messiah, Uzayr and his mother, or groups of jinn, were themselves seeking nearness to their Lord, competing to see who is closest to Him, hoping for His mercy and fearing His punishment. How then could they be worshipped alongside Him? Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Sa'di draw the same conclusion: the one who worships is not himself worshipped, and the one who seeks a means of access to God cannot be petitioned in His place. On the identity of these beings, opinions differ. Ibn Mas'ud, reported in al-Bukhari and Muslim, says they were groups of jinn who embraced Islam without their human worshippers knowing it, and al-Tabari adopts this view while noting another statement from the same companion that identifies them as angels. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid name 'Isa, his mother, 'Uzayr and the angels, and in one transmission Ibn 'Abbas adds the sun and the moon, whereas al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi speak of angels or of 'Isa and 'Uzayr. Ibn Fawrak takes the reference to be the prophets mentioned earlier. On the meaning of wasila, the commentators agree that it is nearness to God through obedience. Ibn al-Qayyim stresses that fear and hope, together with love, are the pillars of worship, while al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur see in placing fear after hope a mark of reverence toward God. All agree that the punishment of God is worthy of being feared.

This verse states a settled decree, written in the Preserved Tablet: every town will be destroyed by God before the Day of Resurrection, or its people will be punished with a severe punishment. The commentators differ on the meaning of the terms. Muqatil, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi distinguish between them: death for righteous towns and punishment for wicked ones, or total destruction on one side and torments such as killing or calamities on the other. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that the verse concerns disbelieving towns that reject their messengers, and that their ruin comes from their sins, a view Ibn Sa'di also expresses. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Shinqiti suggest that an adjective such as "wrongdoing" is implied, supported by other verses saying God did not destroy towns whose people were righteous. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi add that the punishment may be the killing of leaders or the imposition of the poll tax. Ibn 'Abbas links the destruction to the spread of adultery and usury. Almost all agree that the Book is the Preserved Tablet and that the word masturan means written. The report attributed to al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, transmitted by Muqatil, which assigns a fate to each city, is cited by several authors, yet Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Alusi and al-Shinqiti regard it as unreliable and do not adopt it as an interpretation. In the wider context, several scholars (al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi) also explain why God did not send the miracles the Quraysh demanded: their rejection would have brought total destruction, and such signs serve only as warnings. Al-Razi adds that fear moves people to reflect on these wonders.

The commentators explain that this verse answers the Meccans' demand for specific miraculous signs. God states that He withheld them not out of inability, but because earlier peoples denied the signs they had been given and were therefore destroyed. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Jurayj report that the Meccans asked the Prophet to turn Mount Safa into gold, and he was offered either to hasten punishment should they disbelieve or to grant them respite; he chose respite. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the she-camel of Thamud was a clear sign, and that her people wronged themselves by slaughtering her or by rejecting her. The commentators differ on the meaning of the signs in the phrase 'We send the signs only as a warning': al-Hasan takes them to be sudden plague; al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi list miracles, signs of retribution, or the changing stages of life, the last being the view attributed to Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Ibn Kathir and Qatada speak of natural phenomena such as earthquakes and eclipses that God sends to make people reflect. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that the requested signs are a warning of imminent destruction, whereas other signs, including the Qur'an, warn of the punishment of the Hereafter. Al-Razi adds that God knew some of the disbelievers' descendants would believe, which explains the delay.

God reminds His Prophet ﷺ that his Lord encompasses the people, meaning they are in His grip and cannot escape His will, so he should not fear them and must continue delivering his message. Commentators differ on the meaning of encompassing: Mujahid and Ibn Abi Najih take it as God's power, al-Kalbi as His knowledge, while al-Hasan, 'Urwa and Qatada take it as protection from being killed until the message is delivered. Regarding the vision, most scholars, including Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, hold that it was a waking vision of the night journey and ascension, and that some converts apostatised when they heard of it. Others read it as a dream, such as the dream of entering Mecca at Hudaybiyya, the dream of the corpses at Badr, or the dream of the Umayyads on the pulpit; some scholars found these weak given the Meccan origin of the surah. The cursed tree is, for most, the zaqqum tree, cursed because it grows at the bottom of Hell or because its eaters are accursed. Ibn 'Abbas identified it with dodder, while others named the Umayyads or the Jews, a view many consider weak. The people's temptation came from Abu Jahl's mockery of a tree growing in fire. Finally, the warnings only increase the disbelievers in great rebellion.

This verse recalls the moment when God commanded the angels to prostrate before Adam, and all of them did except Iblis, who refused out of arrogance, saying he would not bow to one whom God created from clay. The commentators agree that this refusal stemmed from pride and envy, and that Iblis's reasoning, which prefers fire to clay, is mistaken. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relay from Ibn Abbas that the clay was taken from the surface of the earth, both sweet and salty, which is why some descendants are destined for happiness and others for misery. On the phrase about seizing his offspring, Ibn Abbas and al-Farra' explain it as gaining mastery over them, Mujahid as encompassing them, and Ibn Zayd as leading them astray, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and others understand complete destruction, or leading them as one leads a beast by its bridle. Al-Mawardi lists six different interpretations. As for the exception of a few, Ibn Abbas identifies them as God's protected servants, while al-Hasan suggests Iblis assumed it because he had found Adam irresolute. Most agree that God's command to Iblis to depart and do his worst is a threat and a leaving of him to his own choice, not a permission to mislead. Several commentators extend the means of misleading, the voice, horse and foot, wealth and children, to any call to disobedience, such as song, instruments, usury, or sin in wealth and offspring. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir note that some reports of this kind are weak and not accepted by all. Al-Sha'rawi holds that Iblis was of the jinn who chose to obey, and that his refusal was a deviation.

The verse records Iblis's words after he refused to prostrate to Adam: he challenged his Lord, asking why Adam was honoured over him, then swore that if he were reprieved until the Day of Resurrection he would overpower Adam's descendants and lead them astray, except for a few. On the meaning of 'la-ahtanikanna', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that it means to overpower or to uproot through misguidance, Ibn Abbas says to gain dominion through seduction, Ibn Zayd says to mislead, and Mujahid says to surround. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain it as total uprooting through seduction, while al-Mawardi, al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi also give the image of leading someone by the bridle as a horse is led by its jaw. The commentators agree that the exception refers to those whom God protects and the sincere servants. Some hold that Iblis spoke from supposition, others that he inferred it from the angels' remark about corruption, or from his perception of human nature. Al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan explain that 'arra'aytaka' means 'tell me', and that the sentence implies a rebuke for honouring someone lesser. Al-Baghawi and al-Jaza'iri see the command to go as a rejection and threat rather than real permission. Commentators explain that 'voice' and 'horse and foot' stand for every call to sin and every agent of evil, and that sharing in wealth and children includes unlawful gain and naming children after idols. The commentators do not choose between these views, presenting them as complementary.

The commentators explain that when Iblis asked to be reprieved until the Day of Resurrection, God replied, "Go," meaning: pursue what you have chosen. This is a threat and a rejection rather than a real permission. Whoever among the descendants of Adam follows him will have Hell as a recompense, and it will be a "full" recompense with nothing lacking. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy agree that "mawfur" means complete or abundant, which Ibn Kathir also reports from Mujahid and Qatada. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi note that the pronoun "your" is used because Iblis is the main addressee and includes his followers, and they mention the possibility of a shift to address the followers directly. Most exegetes read the imperatives that follow ("incite them," "muster your forces against them," "share with them," "promise them") as threats rather than real authorisation, and al-Razi and Ibn Ashur describe this as a leaving of him to his own choice. On "voice," Mujahid takes it as singing and musical instruments, while Ibn Abbas takes it as any call to disobedience; al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that the word covers all of these. On "horse and foot," Mujahid and Qatada speak of allies of Iblis among jinn and humans, while others see it as an image for anyone acting in disobedience. Regarding sharing wealth and children, the examples given include illicit gain, usury, offerings made to idols, children born of adultery, naming children after idols such as Abd Shams or Abd al-Uzza, and raising them as Jews or Christians. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir conclude that the verse covers all of these. Finally, the promise is a false one, such as denying resurrection or postponing repentance.

This verse, part of God's address to Iblis after granting him respite until an appointed day, describes the power Satan may exercise over those he can seduce: to provoke them with his voice, to gather against them all his riders and footmen, to share their wealth and children, and to make them empty promises. Commentators generally read the imperatives as threat rather than true permission, highlighting Satan's open enmity toward the children of Adam. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take the voice to mean any call to disobey God, while Mujahid limits it to singing and musical instruments, al-Dahhak to the flute, and others to whispered suggestion. As for the horsemen and footmen, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada say Satan has troops of jinn and humans, and whoever rides or marches in disobedience belongs to them, whereas others take the phrase as a figure of speech for his followers in general. Regarding shared wealth, the scholars mention unlawful gain and its spending in sin, usury, the animals dedicated by the pagans such as the bahira and sa'iba, and offerings made to idols. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir conclude that any wealth used in disobedience to God falls under this sharing. For children, they cite illegitimate offspring, infanticide, raising them as Jews, Christians or Magians, and naming them after idols such as 'Abd Shams. The false promises include denial of resurrection, imagined intercession by idols, and postponing repentance. Some also report narrations about Satan's participation in intercourse when God's name is not invoked, though these are presented as secondary to the verse's meaning.

This verse records God's words to Iblis that he has no authority over His servants, and that the Lord suffices as a guardian for whoever relies on Him. The commentators differ on who the "servants" are. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy identify them as believers, the sincere or the righteous, citing verses such as "he has no authority over those who believe." Al-Razi reports the view of al-Jubba'i that the term covers all the responsible, the exception being stated elsewhere: "except those who follow you among the astray."

Most explain "sultan" as power or the capacity to mislead. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan clarify this, while Ibn 'Atiyya finds the reading as "proof" strained. "Wakil" is explained as guardian, protector, supporter or guarantor. Ibn Sa'di and al-Qasimi see a promise of protection for whoever entrusts himself to God, while al-Alusi notes that the final clause may address the Prophet or the human being rather than Iblis.

The immediate context is God's permission to Iblis to provoke whomever he can with his voice, to gather his horsemen and foot soldiers against them, to share their wealth and children, and to deceive them with false promises. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid interpret the "voice" as the call to disobedience, or as singing and instruments. Several commentators explain that the horsemen and infantry stand for everyone engaged in disobedience. The sharing of wealth and children is glossed as unlawful gain, usury, killing children and false lineage, and Ibn Kathir cites a hadith about invoking God's name before intimacy.

This verse presents God as the Lord who makes ships run for you across the sea, so that you may seek His bounty, and it affirms that He is merciful to you. The commentators agree that « yuzji » means to drive or make flow, and that « al-fulk » is a collective term for ships. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that « His bounty » means provision and profit from trade. Ibn 'Atiyya adds that seeking this bounty includes trade, pilgrimage and military campaign, and that there is no disagreement about the permissibility of sea travel for these purposes, though opinions differ on whether it is obligatory for pilgrimage and whether it is disliked when pursued only to multiply wealth.

Al-Razi and al-Baydawi take the address as general, with mercy meaning the benefits of this world. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi note that the following verses describe human conduct at sea: in danger people forget their idols and call on God alone, but once saved they turn away and become ungrateful. Al-Tabari reads « ḍalla man tadʿūna » as meaning that what is invoked vanishes from the mind, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take the exception as disconnected. The verbs that follow are read in different ways, with some readers using the first person plural and others the third person singular, and the commentators do not choose between them.

Overall, the verse is treated as a reminder of God's favours and a sign of His lordship, which extends to land as well as sea. The polytheists therefore cannot feel safe from punishment by sinking into the earth, by stones from the sky, or by a violent storm.

This verse describes how people behave at sea: when harm strikes and they fear drowning, the idols they normally call upon vanish from their minds, and they call on God alone. Yet once He delivers them safely to land, they turn away and return to associating partners with Him and to ingratitude. The commentators agree on the central point: polytheists turn sincerely to God only in distress, and the verse stresses that man is prone to ingratitude. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the verb "dalla" means to vanish, to be lost or to slip from the mind, while Abu Hayyan and al-Nasafi hold that the exception "except Him" is disjunctive, since the idols were never part of the calling in the first place. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi allow a continuous reading in which people call upon God in the crisis. Al-Zajjaj takes "man" to mean the disbelievers, whereas Ibn Atiyya finds this weak and sees the whole human species. In the following verses, the commentators differ over "hasib": Qatada understands stones from heaven, while Abu Ubayda, Ibn Qutayba and al-Farra understand a wind that carries pebbles. Ibn Kathir recounts how Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl embraced Islam after being saved at sea.

In this verse God addresses those He rescued from the perils of the sea and then turned away from gratitude, asking them in reproach whether they feel safe that He might cause the shore on which they have landed to sink beneath them, or send against them a hasib. The commentators broadly agree on the meaning: divine power makes no distinction between land and sea, and escaping the sea does not guarantee safety on land. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi note that mentioning the 'side' (janib) of the land signifies that all directions are equal before God's power. Lexicographers define khasf as sinking into the ground, and al-Qurtubi describes it as the earth collapsing beneath something. The meaning of hasib is disputed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Mujahid and Qatada take it as a rain of stones, like that which fell on the people of Lot, while Abu 'Ubayda, Ibn Qutayba and al-Tabari report it as a wind carrying pebbles, supported by a line of al-Farazdaq. Al-Zajjaj understood it as dust mixed with gravel, and al-Mawardi also mentions a cloud that pelts with hail or snow. The wakil is explained as the guardian or defender who would ward off such punishment. The commentators see in the verse a reminder that safety on land is a blessing people easily forget.

This verse warns those who turn away from God after being rescued from the peril of the sea. God asks them whether they feel safe from being returned to the sea once more, having a violent wind sent against them that shatters everything, drowning them for their disbelief, so that they find no one to demand vengeance on their behalf.
