The commentators explain that the qasif is a wind so strong that it breaks whatever it passes over. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba understood it as a wind that snaps trees and ships, while Ibn Kathir describes it as the wind of the seas that smashes vessels and drowns them. The word tabi' is glossed by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Farra' as a helper or an avenger, by Mujahid as one who seeks revenge, and by al-Zajjaj as someone who would challenge by denial what has befallen them. Several scholars, including al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi, compare this to the verse stating that God does not fear the consequences. The readings also differ: Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read the verbs in the first person plural, matching "alayna", while most read them in the third person, matching "iyyahu". Some read "fatughriqakum" in the feminine, referring back to the wind.

The commentators explain that God honoured the children of Adam by carrying them on land and sea, providing them with good things, and preferring them over many of His creatures. Most of them agree that this honour applies to the whole human species, the righteous and the wicked alike, and that it is a general quality of the race. They differ on what the honour consists of. Ibn 'Abbas, through Maymun ibn Mihran, is cited by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi as saying that man eats with his hands while other creatures eat with their mouths, a view also reported by al-Kalbi and Muqatil. Al-Dahhak speaks of speech and discernment, 'Ata' of an upright and balanced stature, and Yaman of beauty of form. Al-Tabari gives the subjection of creation to man, and al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi list many further points such as writing, reason, and the fact that Adam was created by God's hand. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi conclude that the true distinction is reason, through which God is known and His speech understood, with revelation acting as a complement that reason alone cannot fulfil. Ibn 'Atiyya argues that the verse mainly sets humans above the jinn and animals, and does not settle their ranking against the angels. Commentators disagree on the word 'many': some read it as excluding the angels, as al-Jalalayn and al-Baydawi note, while others read it as 'all', a reading that al-Razi attributes to Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi set out these positions without deciding between them, and al-Zamakhshari's use of the verse against the Ash'arites is criticised by Ibn 'Ashur as overreaching. Ibn Kathir reports a narrative about the angels' complaint and the reply that God does not equate His creation made by His hand with one made by a word, but notes its weak chain. Several commentators add that the honour can be lost through disbelief, as Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi observe.

This verse describes the Day when God calls every group of people with their imam, meaning the one they followed in this world. The commentators differ on the meaning of imam. Mujahid, Qatada and Abu al-'Aliya understood it as the prophet of each people, and al-Tabari preferred this view because it is the most common usage of the word in Arabic. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Dahhak understood it as the book of deeds, a view Ibn Kathir considered stronger, citing the verse stating that everything is recorded in a clear imam. Ibn Zayd took it to mean the scripture revealed to each community, while others took it to mean the guide, whether good or misguided, or the dominant trait in a person. Those given their book in the right hand will read it joyfully and will not be wronged even by a fatil, the thread found in the cleft of a date stone. Whoever was blind in this life will be blind in the next and even further astray. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari take this blindness to be a blindness of the heart, while Abu 'Ali al-Farisi allows that the second term may mean more blind. Al-Razi and others link the following verse to the pressure exerted by Quraysh and Thaqif on the Prophet, and Ibn 'Atiyya notes that he did not yield, though he came close. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi also mention that the Prophet will bear witness over his community, which does not contradict the role of the book of deeds. Al-Qurtubi cites a hadith from Abu Hurayra about how believers receive their books, and Ibn 'Ashur reads the verse as describing a division according to the path taken in life.

This verse states that whoever is blind in this life will be blind in the Hereafter, and even further astray. The commentators differ on what "this" refers to. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, followed by Ibn Kathir, take it to mean the present world, so that blindness means failing to see God's power and signs. Al-Tabari adopts the reading that it means blindness to the proofs that God alone creates and governs. A narration from Ibn Abbas, cited by al-Baghawi and al-Suyuti, links "this" to the favours mentioned just before, so that blindness to these blessings leads to blindness to the blessings of the Hereafter. Most scholars read the blindness as one of the heart rather than the eyes. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Razi explain that the word is used figuratively for one who cannot find the path to salvation. Al-Hasan holds that a disbelieving sinner in this world will be blind in the next, since repentance is accepted here but not there. On whether the second "blind" is a comparative, al-Farra, al-Zajjaj, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Razi take it as "more blind", while al-Baydawi and al-Biqa'i take it as a greater bewilderment. Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Jaza'iri note that the Hereafter may refer to physical blindness, as in "We shall raise him blind". Al-Sha'rawi holds that blindness of the heart belongs to this world and blindness of sight to the next. All agree, however, that the straying in the Hereafter is the graver, because there is no longer any way to correct it.

This verse says that the idolaters almost managed to turn the Prophet ﷺ away from what was revealed to him, so that he would invent something else against God, and that had he done so they would have taken him as a close friend and ally. The commentators differ on what this temptation was. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that it was the Quraysh's demands, such as touching their idols, or Thaqif's request for a year's delay before abandoning their worship; al-Tabari judges several readings possible without deciding between them. Ibn al-Jawzi cites four reports about the occasion of revelation, and Ibn Kathir considers some of them weak. Ibn 'Atiyya rejects accounts that would attribute to the Prophet an intention contrary to his mission, while al-Razi holds that the reported causes are many and the verse can be read without a specific story.

The commentators agree that God's support preserved the Prophet. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Juzayy note that the word kadat means only near approach, not that he actually inclined toward them. Ibn 'Ashur sees the passage as a reminder of the Prophet's protection from error, and Ibn Sa'di stresses that even the Prophet needed God's steadfastness. The threat of doubled punishment is, for al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi, a warning that does not imply a sin had occurred, while Ibn al-Qayyim links it to the Prophet's high rank. In the next verse, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur take the plan to expel him as a Meccan plot, and God destroyed them soon after at Badr, while Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan also mention Jewish opponents in Medina.

This verse tells us that God steadied His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and protected him from leaning towards the polytheists in the concessions they pressed upon him, so that he never truly inclined towards them. The commentators report that the Quraysh and the Thaqif proposed that he alter part of his message, grant them a delay, or draw closer his poor companions. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, the inclination that nearly occurred was a slight tendency or a passing thought without resolve, and divine protection is a great favour. Al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya set out the different occasions of revelation and note that the Thaqif version is the most debated. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan observe that the verb kada here implies the absence of any inclination, and that the threat of a double punishment, in this life and the next, shows that the fault of a person of high rank is more serious. Al-Razi and al-Mahalli explain that the verb may be attributed to the Prophet by figure of speech, as one says to someone: you nearly killed yourself. Ibn 'Ashur specifies that the double punishment refers to the trials of life and to death itself, and not only to the punishment of the hereafter. Several commentators add that this great protection should move the believer to ask God for steadfastness. The general sense is therefore that the Prophet did not yield, and that the warning applies to all believers.

This verse presents firmness in the truth as a favour from God to His Prophet ﷺ. Had God not made him steadfast, he would have come close to leaning toward the polytheists in what they asked of him. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi, the apparent meaning is that had he inclined, God would have made him taste double the punishment of this life and double the punishment of death, with no helper to save him. Most commentators understand this as the punishment of this world and of the hereafter, with "double" meaning multiplied or especially severe. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari take the word as a description of a punishment, the noun being left out. Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi note that the inclination did not in fact occur. All agree that the threat was never carried out, and that the verse shows the gravity of a fault grows with the rank of the one who commits it, as with the wives of the Prophet. The occasion of revelation is reported in different ways: a delegation from Thaqif asking for delays or privileges, the Quraysh offering a bargain over religious practice, or their wish to stop him touching the Black Stone. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi take the verse as proof that infallibility comes from God, while others read it as a warning against yielding to those who go astray. For the expulsion mentioned in the next verses, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir refer it to Mecca, since the surah is Meccan, while al-Kalbi links it to Medina.

This verse says that the opponents of the Prophet came close to driving him out of the land where he lived, and that had they done so they would have remained only a short time before being punished. The commentators agree on this general meaning but differ on who planned it and which land is meant. Qatada, Mujahid, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others take it to refer to the Quraysh and the land of Mecca. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir prefer this view, because the verses before it speak of the Quraysh and the surah is Meccan. Al-Kalbi, Ibn Abbas and Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm report that the Jews of Medina were meant, who advised him to go to Syria, the land of the prophets, and that the land is Medina. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya judge this report weak, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi mention it without settling the question. Al-Zajjaj reports that the plot was a decision to kill him made at the Dar al-Nadwa, and al-Hasan says the intent was to kill him in order to drive him from the whole earth. As for the short period, Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak link it to the time between his departure from Mecca and the battle of Badr, while others understand it as the length of their lives. The readings "khalfaka" and "khilafaka" carry the same meaning: after you. The verse also states God's constant law that a people who expel their prophet are destroyed, and that this law does not change. Al-Razi notes that the Prophet did not leave under compulsion but by God's command.

The commentators explain that this verse states a fixed divine practice: just as peoples before Muhammad who drove out their prophet were destroyed shortly afterwards, so the Meccans, had they expelled him, would have remained only a little while after him, and no one can alter God's way. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya read this as the destruction of nations that expel their messengers, and they note that it came true when the leaders of Quraysh were killed at Badr shortly after the Prophet's migration, a point also made by al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi. On who is meant by the verb of attempting to expel him, most scholars, including al-Tabari, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qasimi, identify the Meccans, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report a different view that points to the Jews of Medina, which Ibn Kathir considers weak and which al-Razi sets aside because the surah was revealed in Mecca. The readings khalfaka and khilafaka carry the same meaning, "after you", as al-Farra' and Abu Hayyan observe. Ibn Kathir and al-Shawkani regard the narration about a journey to Syria as unreliable. Al-Alusi explains that the accusative sunnah is a verbal noun or an absolute object, and the commentators agree that the verse affirms the steadfastness of God's law and warns against the schemes of those opposed to the Prophet.

The verse commands the Prophet ﷺ to establish the prayer at its appointed times, from the sun's decline after its zenith until the darkness of night, and to maintain the recitation of the Qur'an at dawn. The commentators agree that the verse refers to the obligatory prayers, but differ on the meaning of "dulūk al-shams". Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, Jābir, Qatāda, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and most of the Successors, which al-Ṭabarī prefers, take it to mean the sun passing its zenith, so that the verse covers all five prayers. Ibn Masʿūd, ʿAlī, al-Nakhaʿī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Suddī and Ibn Zayd take it to mean sunset, which points to the maghrib prayer. The first view relies on the hadith of Gabriel leading the Prophet in the noon prayer, the second on Ibn Masʿūd's practice. On "ghasaq al-layl", Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda explain it as the beginning of night, while Abū ʿUbayda and others take it as the thickening of darkness. "The Qur'an of dawn" refers to the dawn prayer, named for the recitation that is a pillar of it, as al-Zamakhsharī notes, and it is the longest in recitation. Most scholars cite the Sahih hadith of Abū Hurayra that the angels of night and day assemble at dawn prayer. The verse then speaks of night prayer, which Mujāhid says is a special obligation for the Prophet, others holding it was once obligatory for him and then became voluntary. The "praiseworthy station" is, for most exegetes, the great intercession on the Day of Resurrection.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to rise for part of the night to pray tahajjud, the prayer after sleep with recitation of the Qur'an, and states that this is an extra devotion for him alone. He promises him a praiseworthy station, maqam mahmud. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi, largely agree that this is the station of intercession on the Day of Resurrection, when the prophets refer the people to one another until the request reaches the Prophet ﷺ. A report from Mujahid says he will be seated upon the Throne; al-Tabari transmits this without settling the matter, while al-Wahidi rejects it strongly as indefensible. On the meaning of nafila, Ibn Abbas holds it was an obligation specific to the Prophet ﷺ, Mujahid holds it raises his ranks since he is forgiven, and others see it as simple surplus merit. On the word tahajjud itself, Alqama and al-Aswad link it to rising after sleep, while al-Hasan places it after the evening prayer. The commentaries also note that the dawn prayer, called the Qur'an of dawn, is witnessed by the angels of night and day. The next verse has the Prophet ﷺ ask for a true entry and exit and a supporting authority, which some connect to the Hijra.

In this verse God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to ask Him to cause him to enter by a sincere entrance, to bring him out by a sincere exit, and to grant him a supporting authority. The commentators differ on what the entrance and exit are. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Zayd, al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir take them to mean entering Medina and leaving Mecca at the time he was commanded to emigrate, and al-Tabari judges this the most correct reading because it follows the mention of the polytheists' plan to expel him. Al-Dahhak understands it as entering Mecca as a victor and leaving it in safety. Others, including Ibn 'Abbas in another report and Mujahid, read it as entering the grave and leaving it at resurrection, or entering the prophetic mission and carrying it out faithfully, or entering obedience and leaving sin. Some hold it to be a general prayer covering every place and affair one enters or leaves. As for the supporting authority, Mujahid takes it as a clear proof, while al-Hasan and Qatada take it as a power and strength by which Islam is supported, al-Hasan recalling God's promise of the rule of Persia and Byzantium. The next verse, 'the truth has come and falsehood has vanished', is explained as the Qur'an against Satan by Qatada, as Islam against polytheism by al-Suddi, and as jihad against polytheism by Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy note that falsehood is bound to perish. All agree that the 'praiseworthy station' of the previous verse is the station of intercession on the Day of Judgment.

God commands His Prophet to declare that the truth has come and falsehood has vanished, for falsehood by its nature has neither stability nor permanence. The commentators differ on what the two terms refer to. Qatada and Ibn Juraj say that the truth is the Qur'an, Islam or jihad, and falsehood is polytheism or Satan. Al-Tabari holds that the truth is whatever pleases God and that falsehood is whatever follows the obedience of Iblis, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Shawkani prefer to generalise the words to every truth and every falsehood. Many authors, including Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, report that the verse was revealed in Mecca and that the Prophet recited it at the conquest, striking with a staff the three hundred and sixty idols around the Ka'ba, which fell on their faces, as narrated by Ibn Mas'ud and Jabir. Al-Qurtubi draws from this the permissibility of breaking idols and instruments of falsehood. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari explain the word zahaqa as departing and perishing, comparing it to the departure of the soul. The commentators largely agree that falsehood cannot withstand truth and that the verse announces the triumph of truth and of Islam. On the following verse, which calls the Qur'an a healing and mercy for believers, some understand healing of hearts from ignorance and doubt, others physical healing through recitation, and Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy consider both meanings possible.

The commentators explain that God sends down from the Qur'an what is a healing and a mercy for the believers: it removes ignorance, doubt and error from hearts and guides them to the truth. It is a mercy for whoever believes in it and acts upon it, while the wrongdoers gain nothing but loss, since their rejection and turning away grow with each new revelation. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi, agree that healing, guidance and clarification are the primary meaning, and that the Qur'an's effect depends on the disposition of the one who receives it. They differ on the particle 'min': Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim take it as explanatory, so that the whole Qur'an is a healing, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi also allow a partitive sense, each revelation answering a particular need. On the kind of healing, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir extend it to bodily ailments through recitation, while al-Tabari and others restrict it to the spiritual. Some, such as al-Razi, understand mercy as guidance, blessing or the expiation of sins. Al-Qurtubi also records scholarly disagreement over amulets and incantations.

This verse describes how a person behaves as circumstances change. When God grants him blessings such as health or ease, he turns away from remembering God and distances himself from Him, as if he had no need of Him. When harm strikes him, such as poverty or sickness, he despairs of relief. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the phrase "nā'a bi-janibihi" means he withdraws or keeps his distance, and al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi add that it signifies arrogance, or serves as an emphasis on turning away. Several commentators, including al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi, take "al-insan" to mean the disbeliever, and al-Qurtubi reports it refers to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi take it as the human species in general, noting that such a trait is common among people.

The commentators broadly agree that "al-sharr" means poverty, illness or hardship, and that "yā'ūs" means one who despairs of God's mercy, as Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said. Ibn Sa'di notes that a guided believer humbles himself in ease and pleads in hardship. Al-Razi observes that a person who prospers may forget God, while one left deprived is overwhelmed by grief.

Regarding the variant reading "nā'a", al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi treat it as a metathesis of "na'a", while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi also mention the sense of rising or getting up. Al-Shawkani explains that this verse does not contradict the verse in Fussilat about the one who prays at length in hardship, since these are different groups of people. Al-Qasimi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the verse describes those who turned away from the Qur'an. The commentators do not derive legal rulings from this verse.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to say that each person acts according to his own disposition, in guidance or in error, and that your Lord knows best who is most rightly guided. The commentators agree on this general meaning, though they differ in how they define the word shakilah. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada render it as side, nature or inclination, and al-Farra, al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba, who link it to the word for form, explain it as way, character or natural disposition. Al-Hasan and Qatada also take it to mean intention, Ibn Zayd to mean religion, and others to mean habit or character. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya judge the explanations of Ibn Abbas and Qatada the strongest. Ibn Kathir sees the verse as a warning to the polytheists, while al-Razi reads in it a difference in the essence of souls: the Quran heals a pure soul and only increases the error of a corrupt one. As for the phrase better guided on the way, al-Razi and al-Nasafi take it to mean the straighter path, while others take it to mean the one more readily accepted. All agree that the final judgment belongs to God alone.

Some polytheists, prompted by Jews, ask the Prophet ﷺ about the ruh, the spirit. The verse answers that it belongs to the command of God, a matter He alone knows, and that human knowledge is little compared with His. The commentators differ on what is meant. The majority, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy, take it to be the spirit that gives life to the body. Al-Hasan and Qatada identify it with Gabriel, Ibn Abbas and Ali with a great angel of many faces, and Mujahid with a creature in human form that is neither angel nor human. Al-Hasan also reads it as the Qur'an. Al-Mawardi lists several opinions, while al-Razi argues that the spirit is a simple, created substance, not a body. On the addressees of «you were given little knowledge», al-Tabari holds that the address is general, since all knowledge apart from God's is small, while others say it targeted the Jews. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim also report the debates on whether the spirit dies and where it goes after death, without settling them. Most commentators link this verse to the verse on wisdom, noting that greatness of knowledge is relative, so there is no real contradiction.

This verse states that God, if He willed, could take away the revelation He sent to His Prophet ﷺ, erasing it from hearts and from copies, and the Prophet would find no one to demand its return or to stand against God. Commentators explain this removal as an erasure from memories and written pages, as al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya do, and some report that Ibn Mas'ud recited it as a warning that a red wind would strip the Qur'an away at the end of time. They agree that the phrase "except by a mercy from your Lord" means God preserved the Qur'an out of mercy toward His Prophet and humanity, which al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy count as a favour extended also to scholars who retain it. Grammarians differ on the type of exception: al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take it as a disjunctive exception meaning "but", while al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan read it as a continuous exception, "unless your Lord shows mercy and returns it". Al-Razi observes that the verse does not prove, as al-Ka'bi argued, that the Qur'an is created, since its removal from hearts does not imply that it began to exist. The following verse, challenging humans and jinn to produce anything similar, is linked by al-Wahidi and al-Qurtubi to demands for miracles from the Quraysh, though commentators do not agree on one specific occasion. Ibn 'Ashur connects the whole passage to the question about the soul and warns scholars against pride in their knowledge.

The commentators explain that the verse follows a hypothetical threat: had God willed, He could have taken the Qur'an away from hearts and codices, leaving no trace, and the Prophet ﷺ would have found no one to plead for its return. God then makes an exception for His mercy, which keeps the Qur'an preserved, and this is counted as a favour added to the gift of revelation. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi read this exception as disjunctive, meaning 'but', while Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan also allow a connected reading, in which God's mercy is what would bring the Qur'an back if it were taken. All agree that God's favour toward the Prophet is great, but they differ on its details. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi cite the sending of revelation, making him lord of the sons of Adam and granting him the praised station, while al-Razi also includes the preservation of knowledge and the Qur'an. Several report sayings of Ibn Mas'ud and Hudhayfa about the Qur'an being lifted at the end of time, though Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi question their soundness. Al-Razi rejects the claim, made by al-Ka'bi, that the verse proves the Qur'an is created. Most read the following verse's challenge as evidence of the Qur'an's inimitability, the impossibility of matching it even by humans and jinn together.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to issue a firm challenge: even if humans and jinn united to produce something like this Qur'an in eloquence, fine composition and depth of meaning, they would not succeed, even if they helped one another. The apparent meaning most commentators give is that the Qur'an's inimitability lies in the creature's inability to match the Creator's speech. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi all read it as a challenge concerning its composition and eloquence. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi add that the inimitability also covers its reports of hidden matters and divine knowledge, while Ibn 'Ashur specifies that it includes eloquence, meanings, moral teachings and laws. Al-Zamakhshari uses the verse to argue that the Qur'an is not eternal, a view Ibn al-Munayyir rejects; Ibn Sa'di, for his part, stresses that the Creator's speech is unlike that of creatures. On the occasion of revelation, Ibn Ishaq reports from Ibn 'Abbas that it concerns some Jews; Ibn Kathir expresses doubts, since the surah is Meccan and its context concerns the Quraysh. On grammar, opinions differ: al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take (they will not produce) as the answer to an implied oath, indicated by the preceding lam, while Abu Hayyan reports the position of the Basran grammarians. The word (zahir) means, for most, a helper or supporter.

This verse says that God repeated and varied in the Quran every kind of admonition, parable and proof for people, so that they would remember and believe, yet most of them refused except to deny. Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Nasafi take the people here to be mainly the Meccans, while others read it as a wider audience including pagans and People of the Book, and Ibn Ashur holds that the definite article in 'the people' is general. Zamakhshari, Baydawi, Nasafi and Abu Hayyan explain that the verb 'refuse' carries a sense of negation, which allows the exception that follows, a construction not possible with a plain positive verb. Razi lists several ways the challenge of the Quran can be understood, whether it concerns the whole Quran, ten surahs, one surah, or a passage, and several meanings of 'parables', including proofs of divine unity and prophethood or the stories of destroyed peoples. Ibn Atiyya places the refusal on human acquisition of disbelief, while its creation belongs to God. The following verses report the demands of the Quraysh leaders for signs, such as a spring gushing from the earth or the sky falling in pieces. Tabari, Baghawi and Ibn Kathir relate this background, Ibn Kathir noting that the surah is Meccan. Tabari prefers the Kufan reading which lightens the first 'tafjur' and doubles the second. The commentators agree that the proof had been made clear and that the refusal came after the truth had become evident.

This verse reports that the leaders of Quraysh, unable to match the Qur'an and faced with the proof already set before them, began demanding miracles of their own choosing. They say they will not believe until he makes a spring (yanbu') gush forth for them from the earth, which the commentators take to mean the land of Makkah, short of water. A yanbu' is a copious spring that never runs dry. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi agree that this is stubborn obstinacy and a stream of demands made after the argument had been established, rather than a sincere search for guidance. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi relay the account of the nightly gathering near the Ka'ba and the proposals made to the Prophet, including a garden, a palace of gold, and an ascent to heaven followed by a written book. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note a difference of recitation over tafjura, with the Kufans reading it without doubling the letter, and al-Tabari preferring the doubled form. Readers also differ on kisafan, depending on whether it means pieces or the whole sky. Ibn Kathir says that the Prophet's request for a respite was an act of mercy, and that one of the demanders, Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya, later became a sincere Muslim. Al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi observe that such demands are not themselves signs of prophethood, since they prove nothing in themselves.

This verse reports what the leaders of Mecca demanded of the Prophet ﷺ before they would believe: that a spring gush from the earth for them, or that he possess a garden of palms and vines with rivers flowing abundantly through it. The commentators agree on this plain meaning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir present these demands as part of a series, and they note that the land meant is Mecca, which lacks water and gardens, as Ibn 'Atiyya also observes. They agree that the demands were stubbornness and obstinacy, made after the proof of the Quran had already been established. According to Ibn Kathir, God knew they would not be guided, so He did not grant them. On the meaning of making the rivers gush, al-Tabari and al-Baydawi understand it as splitting the ground and channelling water, while Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the doubled form suggests abundance. Abu Hayyan and Ibn Juzayy explain that yanbu' is a spring that never dries. Regarding the Prophet's reply, the commentators, including al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, agree that he is a human messenger who does not hold the power to produce such signs, and that the matter of signs belongs to God alone. Some accounts of the occasion of revelation are lengthy, but the central point remains the defiance in the face of clear proof.

In this verse the Meccan opponents ask the Prophet ﷺ to produce miracles of their choosing: to make the sky fall on them in pieces, as he had warned, or to bring God and the angels before them so that they could see them face to face. The commentators agree that the demand was made to test the Prophet and to show stubbornness rather than out of a sincere wish for guidance. On the word "kisafan", some readers vocalize it with a sukun on the sin and others with a fatha; the majority take the vocalized form as the plural of "kisfa", meaning a piece, while the unvocalized form may be a plural or a verbal noun for something broken or covering. The word "qabilan" has two main readings: Ibn Abbas and Abu Salih take it as a guarantor or witness, while Qatada and Ibn Jurayj take it as meaning direct sight and confrontation, which al-Tabari prefers; Mujahid understands it as the plural of tribe, meaning the angels tribe by tribe. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi all set out these meanings. The divine response, as the commentators explain it, is to glorify God and to remind that the Prophet is only a human messenger who has no power to produce signs, which belong to God alone. The occasion of revelation reported by Ibn Ishaq through Ibn Abbas describes a gathering of Quraysh leaders, but this report has a weak chain and some scholars do not accept it as firmly established. The commentaries give most weight to the theme of obstinacy, to the lesson of restraint regarding demands for signs, and to the dignity of the prophetic role.

This verse records the demands that the Meccan polytheists made of the Prophet ﷺ in order to test him. They asked that he have a house of gold, or that he ascend into heaven, and they added that they would not believe in his ascent unless a book came down to them that they could read. The commentators largely agree on the meaning: zukhruf is explained as gold by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, and al-Tabari cites the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, 'a house of gold'. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the word can mean any adornment, and he takes the sky to be the known heaven, while others understand it as the high space above. According to al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, the speaker was Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya, and the whole set of demands, such as making a spring gush forth, dropping the sky in pieces, or bringing God and the angels before them, expresses obstinacy rather than a sincere wish for guidance. The divine reply, 'Glory be to my Lord!', is read by Ibn 'Atiyya as God being exalted above anything imposed upon Him, and by al-Baydawi as a sign of wonder at their demands. The Prophet is only a human messenger who does not hold these signs, which belong to God alone, as al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir point out. Ibn Kathir adds that God knew their stubbornness, and that Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya later became a sincere Muslim. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the reading 'qala' of Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir turns the reply into a narration of the Prophet's words, whereas the reading 'qul' makes it a command.

This verse explains that what kept most people from faith, after guidance had come to them, was not any obscurity in the truth but their objection that God would send a human being as a messenger. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari say this objection came from the Quraysh or from most people, and that the belief behind the words, not merely the spoken words, is what blocked faith. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan suggest the sentence may also be read as a rebuke from the Prophet to his people. The divine reply, which most commentators explain in the same way, rests on the idea that a messenger is sent from among those he addresses, because people feel closer to their own kind and cannot readily receive revelation directly from an angel. Al-Razi argues that if the earth's inhabitants were angels, their messenger would be an angel. Al-Zamakhshari adds that angels living on earth would themselves need a messenger to teach them. Al-Razi also sees God's witness through the miracle as a further answer to the objection, while Ibn 'Atiyya links the surrounding verses to the signs the unbelievers demanded, which God commands the Prophet to answer with the words: glory be to my Lord, was I anything but a human messenger? Al-Sha'rawi adds that delivering a message from God requires intermediaries. The commentators agree on the general meaning, and their differences concern grammar, the occasion of revelation and who exactly is addressed.

This verse reports that the disbelievers of Mecca objected to God sending a human being as a messenger, and God instructs His Prophet to answer that if there were angels walking peacefully on the earth, He would have sent down an angel from heaven as a messenger, since a messenger must be of the same kind as those he addresses. Nearly all the commentators keep to this basic meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan explain that divine wisdom requires the messenger to share the nature of those he is sent to, so that they can speak with him, understand him and receive from him. Ibn Kathir adds that this is a sign of God's kindness and mercy towards people. Al-Mawardi notes that the soul inclines more towards its own kind, and that an angel sent to humans would have been frightening and hard to approach. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi stress that the miracle is enough to establish prophethood whatever the messenger's nature. On grammar, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take (basharan) and (malakan) as circumstantial states qualifying (rasulan), while others read them as descriptions; al-Baydawi and al-Alusi find the first reading better suited to the context. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the verse answers an objection common to all nations that rejected their prophets. Al-Shinqiti and Sayyid Qutb add that a human messenger offers a model of conduct to follow. Al-Alusi discusses at length whether the Prophet was also sent to jinn and angels, citing several views without choosing between them. The commentators agree on the overall meaning of the verse, and differ mainly on details of explanation and grammar.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to tell those who denied that a man could be sent as a messenger that God is sufficient as a witness between him and them, to attest the truth of his mission, the fidelity of his delivery, and their stubborn rejection. God is the One who knows His servants inwardly and outwardly and will repay them for their deeds. The commentators agree that the verse is a consolation for the Prophet and a warning to the disbelievers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu al-Su'ud and Abu Hayyan take the testimony to concern his delivery of the message and the disbelievers' denial and obstinacy. Al-Razi holds that the manifestation of a miracle matching the Prophet's claim is itself God's testimony to his truthfulness. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi follow the same reading, while Ibn 'Ashur understands the witness in the sense of a judge who settles the dispute, as in other verses. According to Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi, the verse was revealed after the notables of Quraysh asked for a witness from among the angels to confirm his prophethood. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi note that the text says 'between me and you' rather than 'between us', to express separation. Sayyid Qutb sees a tone of rebuke and threat.

This verse states that guidance belongs to God alone: whom God guides is truly guided, and whom He lets go astray will find no protectors besides Him. It then announces that on the Day of Resurrection these people will be gathered on their faces, blind, mute and deaf, and that their abode is Hell, whose fire is kindled again each time it dies down. On the plain meaning the commentators largely agree. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that guidance and misguidance rest with God, and that no one can rescue one whom He has left astray. On the phrase 'on their faces' they differ: al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi take it as a literal dragging, relying on the hadith of Anas that God can make them walk on their faces, while al-Mawardi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan read it as an image of haste or humiliation. As for blindness, muteness and deafness, Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan take them to mean they cannot see, speak or hear what pleases them, while Muqatil places them at the moment they are told to be silent. Al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Juzayy also report that they will regain their senses to see the fire and hear its roar. Regarding the fire's dying down, Mujahid speaks of it being extinguished, Ibn Abbas of it subsiding before their bodies are restored, and Qatada of it weakening. Al-Shawkani and Ibn 'Ashur note that this pause does not lessen the torment.

This verse states that this is the due recompense of those who rejected God's signs and who asked, in denial, whether they would be raised as a new creation once they had become bones and dust. Al-Tabari explains that the signs are the proofs and the messengers, and that their words express astonishment at the resurrection. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan read the question as a rejection, treating the resurrection as something they regard as impossible.

Commentators broadly agree on the meaning of key terms: rufat refers to dust crumbled after decay, according to al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, and the signs cover both the Qur'an and the proofs brought by the Prophet. Abu al-Su'ud adds the rational and revealed signs that establish the possibility of re-creation. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi connect the verse to what follows, where God answers that the One who created the heavens and the earth can create the like of them.

On the nature of the punishment, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi tie it to the denial: the fire consumes the bodies and then renews them, so that those who denied re-creation after annihilation endure repeated destruction and renewal. Ibn 'Ashur sees the punishment as fitting the offence, since burned remains are more scattered than the dust of bones. Ibn 'Atiyya also reports that some take being dragged on the face and blindness literally, while others read them as figurative.

This verse tells us that the One who created the heavens and the earth, which are far greater than us, is able to create people like us and bring them back after death, and that He has appointed for them a term about which there is no doubt, yet the wrongdoers stubbornly refuse and persist in denial. The commentators agree that the verse is an argument against those who denied resurrection, and that the word 'see' means seeing with the heart, that is, knowing through reflection. The core point is that human beings are smaller than the heavens and the earth, so bringing them back is easier. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud take 'their likes' to mean a new creation, that is, the resurrection of bodies. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi also allow that God could create other servants who worship Him, though al-Razi himself considers the first meaning closer to the context. On the appointed term, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir say it is death or the Day of Judgment, al-Qurtubi adds the span of life followed by death, and others see it as a reply to the unbelievers' demand that the sky be dropped on them. Ibn 'Ashur explains that 'ajal' may mean the length of life or the moment of resurrection. The verse belongs to a section on the unbelievers' demands for miracles and their doubt that a messenger could be a man, as al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note.

This verse tells the Prophet to say to the idolaters that if they owned the treasures of their Lord's mercy, meaning His provision and blessings including wealth, they would hold back out of fear of poverty, because man is by nature stingy and tight-fisted. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada explain the fear of spending as fear of destitution, while al-Kalbi takes the treasures to be provisions, and al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi understand them more broadly as all blessings. Al-Zamakhshari reads the verb of withholding as meaning simply to be miserly, needing no object. Ibn Kathir and others take the fear to concern the consequence of spending, namely the exhaustion of wealth. The word qatur describes someone who restricts and rations his spending; Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur see it as an extreme form of miserliness. Al-Razi notes that people give mainly seeking praise or return, so they are miserly at heart. Al-Baydawi contrasts human stinginess with God's unlimited generosity. Al-Hasan holds that the verse concerns only the polytheists, whereas most scholars read it as general. Several commentators connect the verse to the Meccans' demand that springs be made to gush for them, explaining that their avarice would make any generosity from them meaningless. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith that God's hand is full and never diminished by spending.

God says He gave Moses nine clear signs proving his prophethood, and the commentators differ on which they were. Most, including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and 'Ata', list the staff, the hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the years of drought and the shortage of crops. Al-Hasan al-Basri counts the drought and fruit shortage as one sign and adds the staff swallowing what they forged, while Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi includes the obliteration of wealth, the splitting of the sea and the stone. Some cite the hadith of Safwan ibn 'Assal, in which the Prophet explains that these signs are the common precepts of all laws, such as forbidding polytheism, theft, adultery, sorcery and usury; Ibn Kathir doubts this report, suspecting confusion with the Ten Commandments. As for 'ask the Children of Israel', most read it as an order to the Prophet to question them so that the truth becomes clear to the polytheists; al-Hasan takes it as reflecting on the Qur'an, and Ibn 'Abbas, in another reading, makes Moses the one asking Pharaoh to release the Children of Israel. All agree Pharaoh accused Moses of being bewitched, but they differ on the meaning: al-Kalbi and Ibn 'Abbas mean deceived or whose mind was affected, al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda mean sorcerer, Muqatil means overpowered, and al-Tabari means one who was taught magic. The reading 'I knew', attributed to 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, has Moses speaking, whereas the majority reading 'you knew' addresses Pharaoh, who in his heart knew the signs were true and denied them out of arrogance.

The commentators explain that Moses answered Pharaoh, who had accused him of being bewitched, by saying that Pharaoh knows well that these nine signs were sent down only by the Lord of the heavens and the earth, and that they are clear proofs of his truthfulness. Most agree that 'basa'ir' means clear evidences and insights. The meaning of 'mathbur' is disputed: Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd take it to mean cursed or deprived of reason, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir to mean ruined or destroyed, al-Farra' and al-Tabari to mean turned away from good and barred from grace, and others to mean defeated. The majority reading 'alimta' addresses Pharaoh, and Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari see in it his obstinacy. The reading attributed to Ali and taken up by al-Kisa'i, 'alimtu' in the first person, makes Moses speak of his own knowledge; al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi find it weaker, and al-Tabari insists that the reading agreed upon by the readers must not be departed from. The commentators note that Pharaoh and his people denied these signs while being inwardly certain of them, as the verse of the Ant states. As for the list of the nine signs, most name the staff, the hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the years of drought and the loss of fruits, while others add the parting of the sea or the obliteration of wealth. The following verse speaks of Pharaoh's plan to expel or kill the Israelites; God drowned him and his people, then commanded the Children of Israel to dwell in the land. The 'promise of the Hereafter' is for most the Day of Resurrection, and 'lafifan' means gathered together in a mixed throng.

The commentators explain that Pharaoh wanted to drive Moses and his people out of the land, meaning to uproot and expel them from Egypt, with some saying by killing and annihilation. But God drowned him and all who were with him. Then God told the Children of Israel to dwell in the land, and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, which is the Day of Resurrection, He will bring them all together in a mingled crowd.

The commentators agree that the word lafif means a mixed throng of different groups in which no one stays apart with his own tribe, and that it signifies all together. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak take it to mean the gathering of all people. Al-Kalbi understands the promise of the Hereafter as the descent of Jesus from heaven, a view also reported by al-Mawardi from Qatada. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi take it to be the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir sees the verse as an early good news to the Prophet of the conquest of Mecca, since its people had planned to expel him just as Pharaoh planned to expel Moses.

Opinions also differ on the meaning of the verb istafazza. Al-Kalbi and Ibn Qutayba take it as to startle or drive out, while Mujahid renders it as to uproot. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi understand it as forced removal, whether by exile or killing. As for the word earth, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi read it as Egypt, while Ibn Atiyya notes it may mean the whole earth depending on context. For the land where the Children of Israel were to dwell, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud identify Egypt and Syria, while Ibn al-Jawzi also cites a view placing it beyond China.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the drowning of Pharaoh and his army. God told the Children of Israel, through Moses, to dwell in the land, which most identify as the land of al-Sham (Syria), while al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir include Egypt as well. As for "the promise of the Hereafter," most of them take it to mean the Day of Resurrection. Al-Kalbi understands it as the descent of Jesus from heaven, Qatada links it to Jesus as well, and Muqatil understands it as the second return of the Children of Israel to the land. All agree that God will gather creation on the Day of Resurrection.

The word "lafif" is read in two main ways. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, followed by Ibn Kathir, take it to mean "all together." Al-Farra' sees it as people gathered from every direction, while al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, al-Zajjaj, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya understand it as mixed groups from different tribes, none withdrawing to its own clan. Al-Tabari also treats it as a verbal noun, and Ibn 'Atiyya expresses doubt about that view without settling it.

Many scholars link the verse to the preceding account. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi tie the land to the land Pharaoh wanted to drive them from. Ibn Kathir sees a foretelling of the Prophet's conquest of Mecca, and Ibn 'Ashur reads it as a warning to the polytheists about the outcome of their plotting. Al-Sha'rawi offers a modern reading connected with the dispersal and later gathering of the Jews, an interpretation none of the other commentators cited adopt.

This verse states that the Quran was sent down with truth and contains truth, and that the Prophet was sent only to bring good news to those who obey and to warn those who disobey. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Ashur, read the preposition bi as meaning accompaniment or connection: the Quran was revealed bound to the truth that justifies its descent, and it came down containing what is true, commands, prohibitions, promises and threats. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi stress its wisdom and its protection from the interference of devils, while Ibn Kathir understands truth as sincerity, justice and preservation.

Regarding farraqnahu, the common reading with a single r means that we explained and clarified it, whereas Ibn Abbas and others read it with a doubled r, meaning that we sent it down piece by piece. Al-Tabari prefers the first reading, which al-Razi and Abu Ubayd also find clearer. On the phrase ala muktin, Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj explain it as slow and measured recitation, while others understand it as a spread over time. Several commentators report that the revelation lasted about twenty to twenty-three years, with variations in Qatada and Ibn Abbas.

Finally, concerning those given knowledge who fall prostrate when the Quran is recited, most identify them as Jewish and Christian believers such as Abdullah ibn Salam, while others name figures like Waraqa ibn Nawfal and Zayd ibn Amr. Some, including Ibn Atiyya, read the passage as a warning as well as a reproach to the unbelievers.

This verse states that God sent down the Quran in stages rather than all at once, so that the Prophet ﷺ could recite it to people slowly and deliberately, and so that it came down piece by piece according to events and the needs of the community. The commentators agree on this general meaning but differ on the verb “faraqnahu”. The majority reading, with a light rā, means we made it clear, explained and detailed it, and al-Tabari prefers this reading because the community agrees on it. Al-Hasan understood it as distinguishing truth from falsehood. Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Qatada read the intensive form, meaning it was sent down verse by verse and surah by surah. Al-Razi and Ibn ʿAtiyya judged the light reading the clearer one, while al-Zamakhshari recorded the intensive reading of Ibn ʿAbbas. On the length of the revelation, Ibn ʿAbbas gave twenty-three years, Qatada twenty, and others twenty-five, a disagreement tied to the disputed age of the Prophet at the first revelation. As for “ʿala mukth”, Mujahid, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd took it to mean reciting slowly and with proper articulation, while others understood it as the extended period of the revelation. On grammar, “qur’anan” is generally taken as the object of an implied verb that the following word explains, following Sibawayh and Ibn ʿAtiyya.

God instructs His Prophet to tell the idolaters who demanded extraordinary signs: believe in the Quran or do not believe. The commentators read this as a threat and a rebuke rather than a real choice, since your belief adds nothing to it and your rejection takes nothing from it. The verse then says that those who were given knowledge before it, meaning the learned among the People of the Book, fall down upon their chins when it is recited to them, glorifying God and acknowledging the fulfilment of His promise to send a prophet. The scholars agree that the verse consoles the Prophet and affirms the truth of his mission. The word for chins is understood as the junction of the jaws, or as the whole face, since that is what touches the ground first in prostration, and the preposition lam is taken to mean on, emphasising specificity. Ibn Abbas, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and most exegetes identify these people as believers among the People of the Book, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and Salman al-Farisi. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and al-Razi add seekers of the true religion such as Waraqa ibn Nawfal and Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl. Al-Hasan says they are the community of Muhammad, while Ibn Zayd holds that the pronoun refers to the Prophet rather than the Quran. On the repetition of falling down, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi explain that the first refers to prostration and the second to weeping. Many exegetes, including al-Qurtubi and al-Ghazali, draw from this the recommendation to weep while reciting the Quran, and al-Shafi'i relied on the phrase Glory to our Lord in prostration of recitation.

This verse describes those who were given knowledge before the Qur'an came: when it is recited to them, they fall prostrate on their faces and say, glory be to our Lord, His promise has been fulfilled. The commentators explain that the promise refers to the sending of the awaited prophet and the revelation of the Qur'an, as foretold in earlier scriptures, and that the prostration is both an act of glorifying God and thanks for the fulfilment of His promise. On who these people of knowledge were, the scholars differ. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya report that they were believers among the People of the Book, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and Salman al-Farisi, while Ibn Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi also mention Waraqa ibn Nawfal and Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl, and Ibn al-Jawzi, citing Mujahid, mentions Jews. On the meaning of al-adhqan, Ibn Abbas and Qatada take it to mean the faces, al-Hasan the beards, and al-Zajjaj explains that the chin is the first part to touch the ground. Al-Tabari prefers al-Hasan's view as closer to the apparent wording, though others do not decide between them. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi stress that the verse belittles the unbelievers and consoles the Prophet with the faith of those better than them. The verb is repeated because the two states differ: prostration, and then weeping and humility at the recitation.

This verse describes people given knowledge who, when the Quran is recited to them, fall prostrate on their chins, weep, and find their humility increased. Commentators agree that it praises such believers and consoles the Prophet ﷺ over the rejection of his people. They differ on who these people are. Al-Tabari takes them to be believers among the People of the Book; al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur name figures such as Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, Waraqa ibn Nawfal and 'Abd Allah ibn Salam. Al-Hasan says they are the community of Muhammad ﷺ, while Mujahid says they were Jews of that time. On the word adhqan, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada understand faces, al-Hasan beards, and al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi the junction of the jaws, the first part to touch the ground in prostration. Several, including al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, explain that the preposition li means upon. The repetition of the verb is explained by the two states: prostration and weeping. Al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di note that the praise of such weeping encourages weeping when reciting. Al-Qurtubi reports the positions of Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i on whether weeping breaks prayer, without choosing among them. Al-Zamakhshari explains that khushu' here means softness of heart and moistness of the eyes.

God tells His Prophet to say to the polytheists that calling upon Allah or calling upon the Most Merciful amounts to the same, since both are names of one Being, to whom belong the most beautiful names. The commentators report that the Meccan pagans objected when the Prophet ﷺ said "O Allah, O Most Merciful", thinking he was calling upon two gods. He is then commanded not to raise his voice in prayer, lest the pagans revile the Qur'an, nor to lower it so that his companions cannot hear, and to seek a middle way between the two. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the word "prayer" here as the recitation during prayer, while Ibn Abbas, Aisha, Mujahid and others take it to mean supplication. Al-Hasan reads it as doing good both openly and in private, neither showing off nor neglecting one's prayer in secret. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the rule applied in Mecca, and some scholars hold it abrogated while others hold it still valid. The following verse is read by the commentators as teaching that all praise belongs to God, who has taken no son, has no partner in dominion, and needs no protector out of weakness, and that magnifying Him means exalting Him above every defect. The Prophet ﷺ called it the verse of honour.

This verse commands the Prophet ﷺ to praise God and declare Him free of having a son, of having a partner in dominion, and of needing a protector against humiliation, and then to magnify Him fully. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir explain that God makes no alliance and seeks no one's help. Al-Kalbi takes the denied protector to mean none from among the Jews and Christians, since they are the most humiliated of people. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl holds that God was never humbled and so has no need of an ally.

Al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy clarify that the protection denied is the kind sought to escape humiliation, while God's loving care for the faithful remains. Ibn al-Qayyim draws out the contrast: God helps out of mercy and not need, whereas creatures serve one another for their own benefit. Ibn Ashur reads the particle "min" as expressing cause, and understands dhull as weakness and dependence.

The commentators agree that praise belongs only to one who has these attributes: a son implies need and finitude, a partner limits power, and reliance on a helper reveals weakness. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Alusi note that these denials, placed under the heading of praise, establish God's completeness and self-sufficiency. Al-Tabari reads the takbir as glorification, Ibn 'Atiyya calls it the strongest word in Arabic for honour, and al-Razi divides it into aspects of God's essence, attributes, acts, rulings and names.

Several reports praise the verse, including that the Prophet ﷺ taught it to the young boys of the Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib and called it the verse of might. Ibn Kathir judges weak the chain reported by Abu Ya'la about curing illness, and rejects claims about protection from theft as unsupported.
